investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Barium gives superior mucosal detail; water-soluble contrast gives less detail but is safe if it extravasates. You accept reduced detail to avoid mediastinitis/peritonitis when a leak is suspected.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is videofluoroscopy (VFSS) and what is it primarily used to assess?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A real-time fluoroscopic video recording of a patient swallowing barium-coated consistencies, performed with a speech and language therapist. It is the reference-standard functional assessment of oropharyngeal dysphagia and aspiration risk.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the difference between laryngeal penetration and aspiration on VFSS?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• Penetration = contrast enters the laryngeal vestibule but stays ABOVE the vocal cords.
  • Aspiration = contrast passes BELOW the vocal cords into the trachea.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is silent aspiration and why is it clinically important?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Aspiration of material below the vocal cords with NO protective cough. It is missed on bedside swallow assessment, carries a high risk of aspiration pneumonia, and is a key reason to request VFSS.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Where does residue typically pool after an unsafe swallow, and why does it matter?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: In the valleculae and piriform fossae. Retained residue can be aspirated after the swallow (post-swallow aspiration).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How does FEES differ from videofluoroscopy?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• FEES uses a nasendoscope for direct fibreoptic views of the pharynx/larynx with no radiation and can be done at the bedside, but has a 'white-out' blind spot during the swallow itself.
  • VFSS uses radiation but visualises the entire swallow including the oral phase and cricopharyngeus.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: A barium swallow shows a dilated oesophagus with a smooth ‘bird-beak’ taper at the GOJ — how is the diagnosis confirmed and treated?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The barium appearance suggests achalasia but is not confirmatory: confirm with oesophageal manometry (gold standard — aperistalsis + failure of LOS relaxation) and do endoscopy to exclude a GOJ tumour (pseudoachalasia). Treat with pneumatic (endoscopic) dilatation, Heller myotomy or POEM; botulinum toxin for those unfit for these.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why must every suspected achalasia have an endoscopy before treatment?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: To exclude pseudoachalasia — a tumour at the gastro-oesophageal junction (or infiltrating malignancy) can mimic the manometric and barium picture of achalasia. Endoscopy ± biopsy rules out cancer before dilatation or myotomy. Suspect it especially with a short history, marked weight loss, or older age.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Where must the naso-jejunal tube tip lie in enteroclysis, and why?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Beyond the duodeno-jejunal (DJ) flexure. This bypasses the stomach and pylorus so the radiologist controls the infusion rate directly, rather than being limited by gastric emptying, allowing rapid controlled distension of the small bowel.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What two agents are infused in enteroclysis and what does each do?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Barium first to coat and outline the mucosa (single-contrast phase), then methylcellulose (or air) to push the barium on and distend the loops, producing the double-contrast effect with superior mucosal and fold detail.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Enteroclysis vs barium follow-through: key trade-off?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• Enteroclysis gives better distension and mucosal detail but is invasive (NJ intubation), less comfortable and less physiological.
  • The follow-through is simpler and better tolerated but relies on gastric emptying and gives poorer, variable distension.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What do you specifically assess on an enteroclysis study?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• Fold pattern (valvulae conniventes)
  • strictures and dilatation with any transition point
  • masses/filling defects (polyps, tumours)
  • and the terminal ileum (classic Crohn's site).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: When should barium be replaced with water-soluble contrast in enteroclysis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: When perforation is suspected or surgery is imminent. Extravasated barium in the peritoneum causes severe granulomatous peritonitis, whereas water-soluble (iodinated) contrast is absorbed safely.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why has the elective double-contrast barium enema been largely replaced?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Colonoscopy (which also biopsies and removes polyps) and CT colonography now give superior mucosal assessment. Barium enema is reserved for incomplete/failed colonoscopy, stricture characterisation, or where endoscopy is contraindicated or declined.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Outline the steps of a double-contrast barium enema.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• Bowel prep (laxatives, low-residue diet) to empty the colon
  • rectal catheter
  • barium instilled then air insufflated to coat the mucosa
  • IV Buscopan (hyoscine butylbromide) to reduce spasm
  • images taken in multiple positions (supine, prone, decubitus, erect).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: When must you use a water-soluble (Gastrografin) enema instead of barium?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
Whenever perforation, leak or obstruction is possible:
  • suspected perforation
  • recent deep biopsy
  • suspected large bowel obstruction/volvulus
  • intussusception
  • and anastomotic-leak checks.
Extravasated barium causes fatal chemical peritonitis; water-soluble contrast is safely resorbed. Exception — toxic megacolon: perform NO contrast enema of any kind (perforation risk); diagnose on plain AXR.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the classic barium enema appearance of colorectal carcinoma?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: An 'apple-core' or 'napkin-ring' lesion: a short, annular, shouldered stricture with irregular margins and abrupt (not tapering) shoulders, in contrast to the smooth, tapered margins of a benign stricture.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How does a contrast enema distinguish mechanical large bowel obstruction from pseudo-obstruction, and what is its therapeutic use in children?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: In mechanical obstruction there is a transition point with no proximal filling; in pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie) contrast flows freely to a dilated caecum. In paediatric intussusception, an air/contrast enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic, achieving hydrostatic/pneumatic reduction under fluoroscopy.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What type of study is a defecating proctogram — structural or functional?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A dynamic FUNCTIONAL study. It films the anorectum and pelvic floor in the act of emptying (rest, squeeze, cough, evacuation/strain) rather than just mapping static anatomy.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What contrast is used and how is the patient positioned for evacuation proctography?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Thick barium PASTE (stool-consistency) introduced into the rectum, optionally with vaginal, small-bowel (oral) and/or bladder opacification. The patient sits on a radiolucent commode and is imaged with lateral fluoroscopy.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is anismus (paradoxical puborectalis contraction) on a proctogram?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A non-relaxing pelvic floor: the anorectal angle FAILS to open (stays acute) on straining, with prolonged or failed evacuation. It is a functional cause of obstructed defecation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How does a rectocele appear on defecography?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Anterior bulging of the rectal wall (into the vagina) with trapping of contrast in the bulge and incomplete/delayed emptying.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the radiation-free alternative to conventional defecating proctography and what is its advantage?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: MR defecography — no ionising radiation and superior soft-tissue / multi-compartment detail. Particularly useful in younger women where pelvic/gonadal dose must be justified.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: A barium enema shows an ‘apple-core’ stricture. What is it and what is the pathway?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: An annular (‘napkin-ring’) colorectal carcinoma. Barium enema is no longer first-line: proceed to colonoscopy + biopsy on a 2-week-wait pathway, then staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (± MRI rectum, CEA) and MDT discussion.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How is paediatric intussusception diagnosed and treated, and when is enema contraindicated?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: US shows a target/donut sign. An air (or contrast) enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic (reduces the intussusception). It is contraindicated if there is peritonitis, perforation or shock — those go to surgery, as does a failed enema reduction.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the main purpose of a hysterosalpingogram (HSG)?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: To assess tubal patency and delineate the uterine cavity contour as part of the female subfertility work-up. Iodinated water-soluble contrast is injected transcervically under fluoroscopy and watched filling the cavity and spilling from the fimbrial ends.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why is HSG performed in the follicular phase (days ~7-10)?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: It is done after menses has finished but before ovulation so an early pregnancy is not irradiated, and because the endometrium is thin, giving a clearer view of the cavity.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What HSG finding confirms tubal patency?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Bilateral free spill of contrast from the fimbrial ends into the peritoneal cavity, dispersing around bowel loops.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is a hydrosalpinx on HSG?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A distal (fimbrial) tubal block seen as a dilated, contrast-filled tube with no peritoneal spill. It is often post-infective and reduces fertility.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What must be excluded/screened for before performing an HSG, and why?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Pregnancy (avoid irradiating a fetus; hence follicular-phase timing) and active pelvic infection. Screen for and treat chlamydia and consider prophylactic antibiotics, because HSG can precipitate a flare of PID.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is a micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG/VCUG) and what phase is most important?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A fluoroscopic study where the bladder is catheterised and filled with water-soluble contrast, then imaged during filling and — most importantly — during micturition (voiding). The voiding phase reveals vesicoureteric reflux and the urethra (e.g. posterior urethral valves).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: List the main indications for MCUG.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• Assessment of vesicoureteric reflux after atypical/recurrent UTI or antenatal hydronephrosis
  • suspected posterior urethral valves in boys
  • bladder/urethral anatomy (diverticula, ureterocele)
  • and neuropathic bladder.
Predominantly a paediatric investigation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Describe the I–V grading of vesicoureteric reflux.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• I: ureter only (non-dilated).
  • II: up to pelvis/calyces, no dilatation.
  • III: mild-moderate dilatation of ureter and pelvicalyceal system.
  • IV: moderate dilatation + tortuosity, blunted calyces.
  • V: gross dilatation + tortuosity + clubbed calyces.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What are the MCUG features of posterior urethral valves?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: In boys: a dilated posterior urethra above the obstruction with abrupt calibre change (the 'keyhole' sign) and a thick-walled, trabeculated bladder. It is an important surgical cause of bladder outlet obstruction in neonatal boys.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which contrast is used in MCUG, and what complementary nuclear medicine tests exist?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Iodinated water-soluble contrast (never barium in the urinary tract). DMSA assesses cortical scarring; MAG3 renogram assesses differential function and drainage. Direct radionuclide cystography is a lower-dose alternative for reflux follow-up.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: After pelvic trauma with blood at the meatus and a high-riding prostate, what must be done BEFORE catheterisation?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A retrograde urethrogram. Blind catheterisation risks converting a partial urethral tear into a complete transection, so image the urethra first.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which contrast agent is used for retrograde urethrography and cystography, and why not barium?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Water-soluble (iodinated) contrast only. Extravasated barium into the peritoneum or perivesical soft tissue causes a severe granulomatous/inflammatory reaction.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: On a cystogram, how do you distinguish intraperitoneal from extraperitoneal bladder rupture and how is each managed?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• Intraperitoneal: contrast outlines bowel loops and fills the paracolic gutters/pouch of Douglas — needs surgical repair.
  • Extraperitoneal: flame-shaped contrast in perivesical/pelvic soft tissue — usually managed with catheter drainage.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What are the three key abnormalities looked for on a retrograde urethrogram?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• Contrast extravasation (urethral disruption/rupture)
  • stricture (record site and length)
  • and false passage (contrast tracking outside the normal channel, often iatrogenic).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why is a post-drainage film important in cystography?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A small extraperitoneal leak may only become visible after the bladder empties, when residual contrast remains held in the perivesical tissues.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is an antegrade pyelogram and how is contrast introduced?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Water-soluble iodinated contrast injected antegradely (from above) into the pelvicalyceal system, via a percutaneous needle puncture of a calyx or an existing nephrostomy tube, to opacify the collecting system and ureter and define the level/cause of upper-tract obstruction.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How does a nephrostogram differ in purpose from an antegrade pyelogram?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A nephrostogram injects contrast down an existing nephrostomy tube specifically to check tube position, patency, and whether the ureter now drains freely to the bladder (e.g. before removing/capping the tube, or checking a stent). The antegrade pyelogram is aimed at diagnosing the level and cause of obstruction.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: When is an antegrade (rather than retrograde) study the preferred way to opacify the upper tract?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: When retrograde (cystoscopic) ureteric access has failed or is contraindicated, and when you need to assess the level and cause of upper-tract obstruction from above.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why must injection during these studies be gentle and at low pressure?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Over-distension of an infected, obstructed collecting system forces bacteria/endotoxin into the bloodstream causing pyelosepsis/urosepsis. Give antibiotic cover and decompress an infected obstructed kidney rather than over-filling it.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: List the main causes of upper-tract obstruction an antegrade pyelogram helps distinguish.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• Stone (impacted calculus)
  • PUJ (pelviureteric junction) obstruction
  • stricture (smooth tapered narrowing)
  • and tumour/extrinsic compression (irregular urothelial filling defect or smooth external compression).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: MCUG in a boy shows a dilated posterior urethra with a ‘keyhole’ bladder-neck appearance — diagnosis and action?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Posterior urethral valves. The obstructing valves dilate the posterior urethra (the ‘keyhole’ sign). Action: relieve with a catheter, monitor U&Es, and refer urgently to paediatric urology for cystoscopic valve ablation. It is the commonest cause of bladder outflow obstruction in male infants.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How does high-grade vesicoureteric reflux look on MCUG, and how does it change management?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Grade IV–V VUR shows a grossly dilated, tortuous ureter with clubbed (blunted) calyces. High-grade reflux risks renal scarring, so a DMSA scan looks for scars and surgical correction (reimplantation) is considered alongside antibiotic prophylaxis; low grades are usually managed conservatively.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How do you tell intraperitoneal from extraperitoneal bladder rupture on a cystogram, and why does it matter?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Intraperitoneal: contrast outlines bowel loops and pools in the paracolic gutters → needs surgical repair. Extraperitoneal: flame-shaped contrast confined to the pelvic soft tissues → usually managed with catheter drainage alone. The distinction directly determines operative vs conservative management.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: A retrograde urethrogram after a pelvic fracture shows contrast extravasation at the membranous urethra — what must you NOT do?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Do NOT attempt to pass a urethral catheter (it can convert a partial tear to a complete one and introduce infection). Establish drainage with a suprapubic catheter and refer to urology. A retrograde urethrogram is the correct first test whenever urethral injury is suspected (blood at the meatus, high-riding prostate, perineal/scrotal haematoma).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: An HSG shows a dilated tube with no peritoneal spill — what is it and how does it steer fertility treatment?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A hydrosalpinx (distal tubal block, usually post-infective/PID). No fimbrial spill = the tube is blocked distally. A hydrosalpinx lowers IVF success and is often clipped or removed (salpingectomy) before IVF; tubal surgery is generally less effective than proceeding to IVF.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: An antegrade pyelogram shows an abrupt cut-off with a dilated collecting system above it — interpretation and next step?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A ureteric obstruction (stone, stricture, or urothelial tumour). The nephrostomy already decompresses the kidney; next steps are to define the cause (CT urogram, ureteroscopy for a filling defect) and relieve the obstruction definitively. Untreated obstruction threatens the kidney (post-renal AKI).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Define a sinus versus a fistula.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• A sinus is a blind-ending, epithelialised tract opening onto one surface only.
  • A fistula is an abnormal tract connecting two epithelialised surfaces or organs (e.g. bowel to skin).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which contrast agent must be used for a sinogram/fistulogram, and why not barium?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Water-soluble iodinated contrast. Barium is avoided because if it tracks into soft tissues or the peritoneum it is retained permanently, causing granulomatous reaction and severe barium peritonitis.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How is a sinogram/fistulogram technically performed?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A fine catheter, cannula or small Foley is inserted into the external opening (Foley balloon can occlude it to prevent reflux); water-soluble contrast is injected gently at low pressure under fluoroscopy, watching the tract fill, with spot views in multiple projections.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What features of the tract do you define on a fistulogram?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• Length
  • depth
  • direction
  • branching/complexity
  • and any communication with a viscus (bowel, bladder), cavity, joint or bone.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the investigation of choice for perianal fistula and what classification does it enable?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: MRI — it shows the tract relative to the anal sphincters and enables the Parks classification (intersphincteric, transsphincteric, suprasphincteric, extrasphincteric) without radiation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the most common modern use of fluoroscopic arthrography?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: As guidance for intra-articular needle placement before MR arthrography (or CT arthrography) — chiefly to detect labral and rotator cuff tears.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: How is intra-articular needle position confirmed before injecting the diagnostic agent?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A small test injection of iodinated contrast under fluoroscopy — correct position shows contrast flowing away along the joint recesses rather than pooling in soft tissue.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Which contrast agent is injected for an MR arthrogram vs a CT/conventional arthrogram?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• MR arthrogram: dilute gadolinium (roughly 1:200) ± local anaesthetic.
  • CT/conventional arthrogram: water-soluble iodinated contrast.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Direct vs indirect arthrography?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• Direct = contrast injected straight into the joint (best distension, standard for labral/cuff imaging).
  • Indirect = IV gadolinium absorbed into the joint over time (no injection, but less distension and less specific).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the key infective complication of arthrography and how is it avoided?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Septic arthritis — avoided by strict aseptic technique; overlying skin infection (cellulitis) is a contraindication.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why is a T-tube cholangiogram performed before removing the T-tube after open CBD exploration?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: To confirm the biliary tree is clear of residual/retained stones and that contrast flows freely into the duodenum. It is classically done around day 7-10 post-op; a normal study allows safe tube removal.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What type of contrast is used for a T-tube cholangiogram, and why not barium?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Water-soluble iodinated contrast, injected gently. Barium is avoided because it is non-absorbable and would be disastrous if there is a bile leak (barium peritonitis / permanent residue in the ducts).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the key safety hazard of a T-tube cholangiogram and how is it avoided?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Over-pressurised injection into an obstructed/infected biliary system causes biliary-venous reflux, provoking cholangitis and septicaemia. Avoided by gentle low-pressure injection, strict asepsis and antibiotic cover.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What abnormalities are you looking for on a T-tube cholangiogram?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• Filling defects (retained stones)
  • duct strictures / calibre change
  • anastomotic or tract bile leak
  • and whether there is free drainage of contrast into the duodenum.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: If a retained CBD stone is found on the T-tube cholangiogram, what is done?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: The T-tube is left in situ (not removed) and the stone is cleared, e.g. by ERCP, or by percutaneous extraction via the mature T-tube tract at around 6 weeks.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What are the two accepted checks for confirming NG tube position, and in what order?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• First-line: aspirate and test pH on CE-marked paper — a pH of 5.5 or less confirms gastric position and the tube can be used.
  • Second: chest radiograph, used when no aspirate is obtained, pH is >5.5, or the patient is on acid suppression.
The CXR must be interpreted and documented by a competent practitioner before feeding.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Describe the correct position of an NG tube on a chest radiograph.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• The tube follows the midline of the oesophagus
  • bisects the carina
  • does NOT deviate into or follow a bronchus
  • and its tip lies below the left hemidiaphragm (in the stomach, ideally >10 cm beyond the GOJ).
A tube veering laterally down a bronchial tree is in the lung — do not feed.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Where should the tip of a PICC or central venous catheter ideally sit, and what is a linogram used for?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Ideal tip position is the cavoatrial junction or lower SVC. A linogram is a contrast injection down the line under fluoroscopy, used when a line won't flush or aspirate, to assess patency, position, kinking, a fibrin sheath, or extravasation/catheter fracture.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is a tubogram and which contrast agent is used?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: A tubogram is the injection of water-soluble contrast (e.g. Gastrografin) down any indwelling tube under fluoroscopy to confirm its position, patency and track before use — e.g. nephrostogram, drain tubogram, gastrostomy check. Water-soluble contrast is used, never barium, because a leak of barium into the peritoneum/mediastinum/soft tissues causes severe inflammation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why is NG tube misplacement classed as a Never Event, and what must never be relied upon?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Feeding into a tube misplaced in the lung is fatal, so under NPSA guidance it is a Never Event. Position must be confirmed (pH 5.5 or less, or a correctly read CXR) before any feed, flush or medication. The 'whoosh test' (auscultating injected air) is unreliable and must not be used.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is myelography (CT myelography) and what does it image?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Imaging of the spinal canal, cord and nerve roots by opacifying the CSF/thecal sac with intrathecal water-soluble non-ionic contrast injected via lumbar puncture under fluoroscopy, usually followed by CT for cross-sectional detail.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Why is myelography now performed only rarely, and in whom?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: It has been largely replaced by MRI. It is reserved for patients who cannot have MRI (pacemaker/certain implants, severe claustrophobia, metal hardware causing MRI artefact) or where MRI is equivocal.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What is the critical contrast-safety rule in myelography?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: ONLY contrast licensed for intrathecal use (non-ionic, low-osmolar, e.g. iohexol) may be injected. Ionic contrast intrathecally (classically gastrografin) is fatal, causing neurotoxicity, seizures and ascending myeloencephalopathy — a classic never-event.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: Outline the technique of a myelogram.
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• Consent (image brain first if raised ICP suspected)
  • lumbar puncture under fluoroscopy into the subarachnoid space
  • inject intrathecally-licensed non-ionic iodinated contrast
  • tilt the table to run contrast up/down the thecal sac under fluoroscopy
  • then proceed to CT myelography.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What signs do you look for on a myelogram?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back:
• Nerve-root sleeve filling defects/cut-off
  • extradural indentation (disc/osteophyte)
  • complete/partial block (define level above and below)
  • cord compression
  • and contrast escaping the thecal sac (CSF leak).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.front: What post-procedure step reduces the risk of seizures after myelography?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.back: Use only non-ionic, low-osmolar contrast intrathecally (ionic agents are neurotoxic and can be fatal), and afterwards nurse the patient with the head elevated (~30°) for several hours so the contrast does not ascend to the head. Also avoid drugs that lower the seizure threshold.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 45-year-old man attends the emergency department after a fall with loss of consciousness, vomiting, and a GCS of 13. What is the most appropriate imaging investigation to detect intracranial injury?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: CT head
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: NICE head injury guidance triages patients with concerning features (reduced GCS, vomiting, LOC risk factors) to CT head, which detects intracranial haemorrhage and injury. A skull X-ray is not used to make this decision, and a normal film would not exclude brain injury.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A skull X-ray in an elderly patient shows multiple small, well-defined lytic "punched-out" lesions throughout the vault. Which diagnosis does this most strongly suggest?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Multiple myeloma
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Multiple well-defined lytic "punched-out" lesions are the classic skull appearance of multiple myeloma. Paget's gives "cotton wool" sclerosis, hyperparathyroidism a granular "pepperpot" skull, and thalassaemia a "hair-on-end" pattern.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A skull X-ray is requested as part of the assessment of a 6-month-old infant with unexplained bruising and a suspicious limb fracture. What is the primary reason the skull film is being taken here?
options: As part of a skeletal survey for suspected non-accidental injury
To assess the sella turcica for a pituitary tumour
To confirm the child is safe for discharge
To detect a ventriculoperitoneal shunt blockage
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: As part of a skeletal survey for suspected non-accidental injury
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: In suspected non-accidental injury the skull is imaged as part of a full paediatric skeletal survey looking for occult fractures. Intracranial injury would be assessed with CT/MRI, and safeguarding referral is mandatory. The skull film cannot clear a child for discharge.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 24-year-old is assaulted and has left facial swelling. The OM radiograph shows a soft-tissue "teardrop" projecting from the orbital floor into the maxillary antrum, with opacification of the sinus. He reports double vision on looking up. Which fracture is most likely?
options: Orbital blowout fracture of the floor
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Orbital blowout fracture of the floor
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The teardrop sign (herniated orbital contents in the antral roof), antral opacification and diplopia on upgaze from inferior rectus tethering are classic for an orbital floor blowout fracture.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: When reviewing a facial X-ray using McGrigor–Campbell lines, which structures does line 2 cross?
options: Zygomatic arches, inferior orbital margins and maxillary antra
Zygomatico-frontal sutures and superior orbital margins
Mandibular condyles and the occlusal line
Nasal bones and anterior nasal spine
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Zygomatic arches, inferior orbital margins and maxillary antra
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Line 1 runs across the zygomatico-frontal sutures/superior orbital margins, line 2 across the zygomatic arches, inferior orbital margins and maxillary antra, and line 3 across the mandibular condyles and occlusal line.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with facial trauma has a tense, proptosed, painful eye and rapidly falling visual acuity after their injury. What is the most important immediate concern?
options: Le Fort I fracture with malocclusion
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Retrobulbar haemorrhage
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A tense, proptosed, painful eye with falling acuity after trauma indicates retrobulbar haemorrhage, a sight-threatening emergency requiring immediate orbital decompression, not further plain imaging.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 22-year-old is punched in the nose. There is swelling and mild deviation but no epistaxis now, no CSF leak, and no other injury. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Request lateral nasal and OM X-rays to confirm the fracture
Arrange an urgent CT of the facial bones
Immediately manipulate the nasal bones under anaesthesia
Discharge with no examination as nasal fractures are trivial
Examine inside the nose, then plan clinical review at 5–7 days
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Examine inside the nose, then plan clinical review at 5–7 days
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A simple nasal fracture is a clinical diagnosis and X-ray does not change management. You must examine the septum for a haematoma, then review at 5–7 days once swelling settles to assess deformity. CT is reserved for suspected skull base injury.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On examining a patient after nasal trauma you find a boggy, bilateral swelling on the nasal septum. What is the correct action?
options: Prescribe oral antibiotics alone and discharge
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Urgent incision and drainage
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is a septal haematoma — the must-not-miss injury. Untreated it causes septal cartilage necrosis/abscess and saddle-nose deformity, so it requires urgent incision and drainage, not delay or imaging.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with facial trauma has clear fluid dripping from one nostril that forms a 'halo/tramline' sign on tissue. Which statement is correct?
options: A nasal X-ray will confirm the diagnosis
This indicates a septal haematoma requiring drainage
It is expected after any nasal fracture and needs no action
Beta-2-transferrin testing and CT with neurosurgical input are indicated
Manipulation of the nasal bones should be performed urgently
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Beta-2-transferrin testing and CT with neurosurgical input are indicated
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Clear rhinorrhoea with a halo/tramline sign suggests CSF leak from a cribriform plate/anterior skull base fracture. It is confirmed with beta-2-transferrin and imaged with CT, with neurosurgical involvement — a nasal X-ray has no role.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 22-year-old is assaulted and has a fracture of the right mandibular body confirmed on OPG. What is the single most important next step in interpreting the film?
options: Deliberately search for a second (often contralateral) fracture
Conclude the assessment as one fracture is identified
Request an urgent CT head for intracranial injury
Measure the degree of dental caries present
Assess the maxillary sinuses for a fluid level
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Deliberately search for a second (often contralateral) fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The mandible is a bony ring, so fractures are frequently in two places. A right body fracture classically pairs with a contralateral condylar or angle fracture — missing the second fracture is a common exam and clinical trap.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which mandibular fracture pattern is most likely to compromise the airway?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Bilateral anterior (parasymphyseal, 'bucket-handle') fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A bilateral anterior fracture frees the central fragment; the tongue attached to it can fall backwards and obstruct the airway — a true emergency requiring immediate airway management.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognised sign of a mandibular fracture on imaging or examination?
options: A lucent line crossing the cortex
A step in the lower-border cortex
A tooth lying within the fracture line
Uniform widening of the periodontal ligament of all teeth
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Uniform widening of the periodontal ligament of all teeth
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Fracture signs are a lucent line, a cortical step (especially at the lower border), malocclusion, and a tooth in the fracture line. Generalised uniform periodontal ligament widening is not a fracture sign.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 3-year-old presents drooling, toxic and sitting forward with muffled voice and rapidly worsening stridor. A junior colleague suggests obtaining a lateral soft tissue neck X-ray to look for the thumbprint sign. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Send the child to the X-ray department for a lateral neck film
Keep the child calm and upright and summon senior anaesthetic and ENT help to secure the airway
Lie the child flat and examine the throat with a tongue depressor
Give oral antibiotics and reassess in one hour
Perform flexible nasendoscopy at the bedside without preparation
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Keep the child calm and upright and summon senior anaesthetic and ENT help to secure the airway
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is suspected epiglottitis — an airway emergency. Do not distress the child, examine the throat, lie them flat, or send for imaging, as any of these may precipitate complete airway obstruction. The priority is a secured airway with senior anaesthetic/ENT support before any investigation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On a correctly performed lateral soft tissue neck radiograph, which finding best supports a diagnosis of retropharyngeal abscess?
options: A radiolucent fish bone in the vallecula
Prevertebral soft tissue wider than the adjacent vertebral body, possibly with gas or an air-fluid level
Narrowing of the piriform fossae bilaterally
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Prevertebral soft tissue wider than the adjacent vertebral body, possibly with gas or an air-fluid level
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Retropharyngeal abscess widens the prevertebral soft tissues (rough rule >~7 mm at C2, >~14–22 mm at C6), sometimes with gas or an air-fluid level, and the child holds the neck extended. The steeple sign is croup (and a frontal-view sign), the swollen epiglottis is epiglottitis, and radiolucent bones are not seen on plain film.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A lateral neck film reported as showing 'widened prevertebral soft tissues' was taken while the child was crying with the neck flexed. Before referring for suspected retropharyngeal abscess, what is the most important next step?
options: Repeat the film in inspiration with the neck extended
Immediately drain the collection in the emergency department
Request an urgent CT with contrast without any further plain films
Reassure and discharge as the finding is always artefactual
Start intravenous steroids for presumed croup
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Repeat the film in inspiration with the neck extended
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Flexion and expiration falsely widen the prevertebral soft tissues and are a classic pitfall. A film taken in inspiration with the neck extended should be obtained to confirm genuine widening before escalating. The apparent swelling may resolve on a correctly performed film, avoiding unnecessary intervention.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A head-injured patient has periorbital bruising, mastoid bruising and clear fluid from the nose. Which is the correct investigation?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: CT head
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Panda eyes + Battle’s sign + CSF rhinorrhoea indicate a base-of-skull fracture. Imaging is a CT head (skull X-rays are obsolete for head injury under NICE guidance).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A child is drooling, tripoding and has stridor. A lateral neck film shows a thumbprint sign. What is the priority?
options: Lie the child flat for a better X-ray
Examine the throat with a tongue depressor
Secure the airway with senior anaesthetic/ENT support
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Secure the airway with senior anaesthetic/ENT support
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The thumbprint sign indicates epiglottitis. The priority is the airway: do NOT distress the child, lie them flat, or examine the throat (can precipitate complete obstruction). Get senior anaesthetics/ENT to secure the airway, then IV antibiotics.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 25-year-old is brought in after a high-speed motorbike crash with midline cervical tenderness and paraesthesiae in both hands. What is the most appropriate cervical spine imaging?
options: No imaging — apply NEXUS and discharge
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: CT cervical spine
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is significant trauma with high-risk features (dangerous mechanism, paraesthesiae). NICE/modern practice favours CT over plain films because plain films miss injuries. The Canadian C-Spine Rule mandates imaging here, and CT is the correct modality.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A junior doctor reports a 'normal' lateral cervical spine film in a trauma patient, but the image only shows down to C6. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Clear the cervical spine and remove the collar
Accept the film as adequate and discharge
Repeat the same lateral view once more only
Reassure the patient and arrange outpatient MRI
Regard the film as inadequate and obtain further imaging (e.g. CT) while keeping the neck immobilised
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Regard the film as inadequate and obtain further imaging (e.g. CT) while keeping the neck immobilised
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: An adequate lateral must show C1 to the C7/T1 junction. Injuries at the cervicothoracic junction are commonly missed. You cannot clear a c-spine on an inadequate film — keep it immobilised and image further, typically with CT.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On an open-mouth (peg) view, the lateral masses of C1 are splayed laterally beyond the margins of C2 following an axial-loading injury. Which fracture does this suggest?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Jefferson (C1 burst) fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A Jefferson fracture is a burst fracture of the C1 ring from axial loading. On the peg/open-mouth view the C1 lateral masses are displaced outward (overhang) relative to C2, which is the classic sign.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which single finding on a lateral cervical radiograph is a soft-tissue clue to an occult underlying fracture?
options: Preservation of the normal cervical lordosis
Symmetrical C1 lateral masses on the peg view
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Prevertebral soft tissue widening
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Prevertebral soft tissue widening reflects blood/oedema anterior to the vertebrae and can be the only clue to an occult fracture. The other options are all normal/reassuring findings.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 78-year-old woman presents with sudden mid-back pain after bending down. AP and lateral thoracic radiographs show anterior wedging of a mid-thoracic vertebral body with loss of anterior height, preserved endplate cortex and two intact symmetric pedicles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Osteoporotic wedge compression fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Anterior wedging with preserved endplate cortex and intact pedicles in an elderly patient after minor trauma is the classic picture of a benign osteoporotic compression fracture. Pedicle destruction or an unusual level would raise concern for a pathological/metastatic cause.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On an AP thoracic spine radiograph, one vertebra is noted to have only a single visible pedicle, with the other pedicle absent. What does this "winking owl" sign most strongly suggest?
options: Metastatic destruction of the pedicle by tumour
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Metastatic destruction of the pedicle by tumour
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The paired pedicles resemble an owl's eyes on the AP view; loss of one (the winking owl / absent pedicle sign) reflects bony destruction, classically metastatic tumour, and warrants urgent further imaging and investigation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 60-year-old man with known prostate cancer reports 3 weeks of thoracic back pain, worse at night, with new lower-limb weakness and difficulty passing urine. His thoracic spine X-ray appears unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and discharge as the film is normal
Prescribe simple analgesia and review in 6 weeks
Repeat the plain film in 2 weeks
Urgent whole-spine MRI with dexamethasone and specialist referral
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Urgent whole-spine MRI with dexamethasone and specialist referral
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Red flags (cancer history, night pain, neurology, bladder dysfunction) point to metastatic spinal cord compression. A normal plain film does not exclude it; management is urgent whole-spine MRI, dexamethasone and oncology/spinal referral, never reassurance from an X-ray.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 34-year-old man presents with 8 weeks of non-specific low back pain, no red flag features and a normal neurological examination. What is the most appropriate imaging?
options: AP and lateral lumbosacral spine X-ray
No imaging — reassure and manage conservatively
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: No imaging — reassure and manage conservatively
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: NICE advises against routine imaging for non-specific low back pain without red flags. Plain films carry a significant gonadal dose and rarely change management; MRI is reserved for suspected serious pathology. Management is reassurance, activity advice, analgesia and safety-netting.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with acute bilateral leg pain, saddle numbness, and difficulty passing urine. Examination shows reduced anal tone. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Request AP and lateral lumbosacral radiographs
Prescribe analgesia and review in 2 weeks
Arrange urgent MRI of the spine and refer to spinal surgery
Request a CT lumbar spine as first-line
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Arrange urgent MRI of the spine and refer to spinal surgery
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: These features indicate cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency. Urgent MRI and immediate spinal surgery referral are required. A plain X-ray is useless and must not delay definitive imaging and decompression.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An oblique lumbar spine radiograph shows a "collar" across the neck of the Scottie dog at L5. Which abnormality does this represent?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Pars interarticularis defect (spondylolysis)
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The neck of the Scottie dog corresponds to the pars interarticularis; a break or "collar" across it indicates spondylolysis. If bilateral, this can permit a forward slip (spondylolisthesis), but the collar sign itself denotes the pars defect.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 34-year-old woman attends A&E with isolated coccygeal pain after slipping and landing on her buttocks. She is neurologically intact with focal tenderness over the coccyx. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Request an AP and lateral coccyx X-ray to confirm a fracture before treating
Arrange urgent MRI of the sacrum and coccyx
Reassure, provide analgesia and a ring cushion, and advise on activity modification without imaging
Refer for CT of the pelvis to exclude a pelvic ring injury
Admit for orthopaedic surgical fixation of the coccyx
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Reassure, provide analgesia and a ring cushion, and advise on activity modification without imaging
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Coccydynia is largely a clinical diagnosis and a coccygeal fracture is managed conservatively regardless of X-ray findings. A coccyx film therefore rarely changes management and cannot justify its pelvic/gonadal radiation dose. There is no high-energy mechanism or neurological deficit to warrant CT/MRI or surgery.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An 82-year-old woman with osteoporosis develops progressive low sacral/buttock pain over two weeks with no injury. A plain sacral radiograph is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure her that the normal film excludes a fracture
Prescribe a coccyx ring cushion and discharge
Request a repeat plain film in six weeks
Start empirical antibiotics for suspected osteomyelitis
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Arrange MRI of the sacrum
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: New sacral pain in an elderly osteoporotic patient should raise suspicion of a sacral insufficiency fracture (or metastasis). These are frequently occult on plain film, so a normal radiograph does not exclude them; MRI is the sensitive investigation of choice.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 26-year-old man is brought in after a motorcycle collision. He has posterior pelvic pain and a sacral fracture is suspected as part of a pelvic ring injury. Which assessment is most important to perform urgently?
options: Measurement of coccygeal angulation on a lateral film
Assessment of perineal sensation and continence
Range of movement at both hips
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Assessment of perineal sensation and continence
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A sacral fracture within a high-energy pelvic ring injury may be unstable and can injure the cauda equina or sacral plexus. Assessing perineal (saddle) sensation and continence screens for this neurological injury and, together with concern for haemorrhage, mandates urgent orthopaedic/pelvic-trauma input.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A restrained passenger in a head-on collision has a horizontal fracture through a lumbar vertebra. Besides the spinal injury, what must be excluded?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Intra-abdominal (bowel/mesenteric) injury
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is a Chance (seatbelt/flexion-distraction) fracture. It is strongly associated with intra-abdominal injuries (bowel, mesentery, pancreas), so a CT abdomen is needed to exclude them.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A man with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis has neck pain after a minor fall. Why is this high-risk?
options: A fused (ankylosed) spine fractures with trivial trauma and is highly unstable
Ankylosing spondylitis protects the spine from fracture
The X-ray will always show the fracture clearly
It is never associated with neurological injury
Only the sacroiliac joints can be affected
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: A fused (ankylosed) spine fractures with trivial trauma and is highly unstable
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: An ankylosed spine behaves like a long bone: even minor trauma can cause an unstable transverse fracture through the fused segments, with a high risk of cord injury. Have a low threshold for CT/MRI even with a trivial mechanism.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A chest radiograph shows the medial ends of the clavicles unequally spaced from the spinous processes of the thoracic vertebrae. Which aspect of image quality is inadequate?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Rotation
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Adequate rotation is confirmed when the spinous processes lie equidistant between the medial ends of the clavicles. Unequal spacing means the patient is rotated, which distorts mediastinal and cardiac contours and can mimic or mask pathology.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient's PA chest film shows loss of the right heart border with adjacent air-space opacification. Which lobe is most likely affected?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Right middle lobe
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: By the silhouette sign, loss of the right heart border indicates pathology in the anatomically adjacent right middle lobe. Right lower lobe consolidation instead effaces the right hemidiaphragm, not the heart border.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A young man presents with sudden breathlessness, hypotension, a trachea deviated to the left, and absent breath sounds on the right. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Request an urgent portable chest X-ray before treating
Immediate needle decompression of the right chest
Insert a formal intercostal chest drain after imaging
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Immediate needle decompression of the right chest
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is a tension pneumothorax — a clinical diagnosis. Treatment must not be delayed for imaging; immediate decompression (needle then chest drain) is life-saving. Waiting for a CXR risks fatal cardiovascular collapse.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On a PA chest radiograph, which finding most specifically suggests a perforated abdominal viscus?
options: A meniscus at the lung base
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Free air under the diaphragm
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Free gas beneath the hemidiaphragm (pneumoperitoneum) on an erect film indicates a perforated viscus and mandates urgent surgical review. Costophrenic blunting and a meniscus indicate effusion; hilar enlargement suggests lymphadenopathy.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: When assessing inspiration quality on a PA chest film, how many posterior ribs should be visible above the diaphragm in an adequate film?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Adequate inspiration is shown by 8–10 posterior ribs (or 5–6 anterior ribs) visible above the diaphragm. A poorer inspiratory effort crowds the basal lung markings and can mimic consolidation or cardiomegaly.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 72-year-old ICU patient has an AP portable supine chest film. The cardiac silhouette looks enlarged with a cardiothoracic ratio well above 50%. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Report definite cardiomegaly and start diuresis
Apparent cardiomegaly is unreliable on an AP film due to magnification; correlate with a PA film or echo
Conclude the film is technically inadequate and cannot be reported at all
Report biventricular failure on the basis of heart size
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Apparent cardiomegaly is unreliable on an AP film due to magnification; correlate with a PA film or echo
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: On an AP projection the heart lies further from the film and is magnified, so the cardiothoracic ratio cannot be used to diagnose cardiomegaly. The correct response is to note apparent enlargement is unreliable and correlate with a PA film or echocardiography, not to act on the measurement.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A nurse asks you to confirm an NG tube is safe for feeding on a portable chest X-ray. Which single finding confirms correct placement?
options: The tube tip lies at the level of the carina
The tube deviates to the right at the level of the aortic arch
The tube tip is seen in the right lower zone
The tube follows the line of a bronchus
The tube bisects the carina, passes below the left hemidiaphragm and the tip is in the stomach
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: The tube bisects the carina, passes below the left hemidiaphragm and the tip is in the stomach
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Safe NG placement requires the tube to bisect the carina, remain midline, cross below the left hemidiaphragm and have its tip clearly within the stomach. Feeding through a tube whose tip is in the lungs is a fatal never event, so any bronchial course must be excluded before feed is given.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A ventilated patient in resus has a supine AP film. There is an abnormally deep, lucent, sharply outlined right costophrenic angle but no obvious apical lung edge. What does this most likely represent?
options: A pneumothorax shown by the deep sulcus sign
Free gas under the diaphragm from a perforation
Consolidation of the right lower lobe
Normal appearance for a supine film
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: A pneumothorax shown by the deep sulcus sign
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: When a patient is supine, pneumothorax air rises to the anterior and basal chest rather than the apex, so the usual apical lung edge is absent. The deep sulcus sign — an abnormally deep, lucent costophrenic angle — is the key clue to a pneumothorax on a supine AP film. A layering effusion causes diffuse haziness, not a lucent sulcus.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A PA chest film shows a subtle opacity that seems to lie behind the cardiac shadow. A lateral is obtained to localise it. Which structures on the lateral are used to assign a lesion to a specific lobe?
options: The aortic knuckle and the azygos vein
The costophrenic angles and the gastric bubble
The oblique (major) fissures, plus the horizontal (minor) fissure on the right
The tracheal air column and carina
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: The oblique (major) fissures, plus the horizontal (minor) fissure on the right
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The obliquely running major fissures divide upper/middle from lower lobes; the right horizontal fissure separates right upper from right middle lobe. Relating the lesion to these fissures on the lateral assigns it to a lobe in the antero-posterior plane that the PA cannot resolve.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On a lateral chest radiograph you notice the lower thoracic vertebral bodies appear whiter (denser) than the upper ones. What does this 'spine sign' most suggest?
options: Lower lobe pathology such as consolidation, collapse or effusion
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Lower lobe pathology such as consolidation, collapse or effusion
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Normally the vertebrae become progressively more lucent (darker) inferiorly as soft tissue thins out. Increasing density towards the lower spine (a positive spine sign) indicates superimposed lower lobe pathology projected over the vertebral column.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A young adult's lateral chest film shows loss of the normal lucency in the retrosternal clear space. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate concern and next step?
options: A small anterior pneumothorax; discharge with advice
Left lower lobe collapse; repeat the PA in one week
An anterior mediastinal mass (e.g. lymphoma/thymoma); arrange CT for urgent characterisation
A normal thymic remnant; no further action
A large pleural effusion; therapeutic aspiration on the ward
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: An anterior mediastinal mass (e.g. lymphoma/thymoma); arrange CT for urgent characterisation
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The retrosternal clear space is normally lucent; filling it in (increased whiteness) points to an anterior mediastinal mass — the 'terrible Ts'. In a young adult lymphoma is a key concern, and a mass here can threaten the airway or SVC, so urgent cross-sectional imaging with CT is warranted.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient has a suspected small apical pneumothorax not clearly seen on the inspiratory film. Why can an expiratory film help?
options: The pneumothorax expands as the patient breathes out
Expiration increases pleural air pressure and enlarges the pneumothorax
The heart moves and uncovers the apex
Expiration reduces the density of the lung, making air easier to see
Lung volume falls while the pneumothorax volume stays constant, making it relatively larger and more conspicuous
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Lung volume falls while the pneumothorax volume stays constant, making it relatively larger and more conspicuous
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: On expiration the lung deflates but the trapped pleural air does not, so the pneumothorax occupies a proportionally larger fraction of a smaller, denser hemithorax and becomes easier to detect. Note that BTS guidance regards routine expiratory films as adding little over a good inspiratory film.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 3-year-old presents after a choking episode. An expiratory CXR is requested for suspected inhaled foreign body. Which finding best supports the diagnosis?
options: Unilateral hyperinflation with the affected lung staying lucent and the mediastinum shifting away on expiration
The affected lung deflates more than the normal lung
A visible visceral pleural line at the apex
Complete white-out of the affected hemithorax
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Unilateral hyperinflation with the affected lung staying lucent and the mediastinum shifting away on expiration
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A ball-valve foreign body lets air in but not out, so the obstructed lung cannot deflate on expiration. It stays lucent while the normal lung empties, and the mediastinum shifts away from the affected side — the contrast is greatest on the expiratory film.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A trauma patient is hypotensive with a deviated trachea, distended neck veins and a hyperresonant, silent right chest. What is the correct next step?
options: Request an urgent portable chest X-ray to confirm
Observe on high-flow oxygen and repeat imaging
Insert a formal chest drain after the X-ray
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Immediate needle or finger decompression
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is tension pneumothorax — a clinical diagnosis and immediate life threat. Treatment must not be delayed by imaging: perform emergency needle/finger decompression at once, then a definitive chest drain. You do NOT wait for or request a chest X-ray.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 40-year-old man attends after falling against a bannister. He is comfortable, saturating 98% on air, with focal tenderness over a left lateral rib. Chest is clear on auscultation. What is the most appropriate imaging approach?
options: Standard erect chest X-ray to exclude complications
Dedicated left rib views to confirm and count the fractures
CT chest to grade the fracture
No imaging is ever needed in chest trauma
Repeat rib views in 10 days to check healing
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Standard erect chest X-ray to exclude complications
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Dedicated rib views do not change management of a simple fracture and miss fractures anyway. The value of imaging is a standard CXR to detect pneumothorax, haemothorax, contusion or surgical emphysema.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which finding best defines flail chest?
options: A single rib fractured in two places
Two adjacent ribs each fractured once
Three or more consecutive ribs each fractured in two or more places
Any fracture of the first rib
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Three or more consecutive ribs each fractured in two or more places
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This frees a chest-wall segment that moves paradoxically. It is a clinical diagnosis associated with underlying lung contusion and respiratory compromise, and may need ventilatory support.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A cyclist hit by a car has a fractured left 10th and 11th rib. Beyond analgesia, what is the priority concern?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Splenic and renal injury
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Lower rib fractures (9–12) overlie solid organs: left-sided fractures risk splenic injury and either side risks renal injury (right-sided risk liver). Assess with CT/FAST for intra-abdominal injury.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 34-year-old is brought in after a high-speed RTC in which his chest struck the steering wheel. A lateral sternum view shows a cortical step in the sternal body. He is haemodynamically stable. Which is the single most important immediate investigation to exclude a dangerous associated injury?
options: Repeat plain sternal radiograph in 24 hours
12-lead ECG and troponin with cardiac monitoring
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: 12-lead ECG and troponin with cardiac monitoring
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A sternal fracture is a marker of significant anterior chest trauma. The key concern is blunt cardiac injury (myocardial contusion) with its arrhythmia risk, so an ECG, troponin and a period of cardiac monitoring are mandated. The other options address non-traumatic or non-urgent issues.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: In a patient with significant blunt anterior chest trauma and a suspected sternal fracture, why is CT chest generally preferred over dedicated plain sternal views?
options: CT uses a lower radiation dose than plain film
Plain film cannot show any bony fracture
CT is the only test that can diagnose myeloma
CT images the sternum and the associated cardiac, vascular, pulmonary and spinal injuries far better
Plain film requires the patient to be prone, which is impossible in trauma
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: CT images the sternum and the associated cardiac, vascular, pulmonary and spinal injuries far better
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: CT is superior for the sternum itself and, crucially, for the associated injuries that actually matter — myocardial contusion, pericardial effusion, great-vessel injury, pulmonary contusion and thoracic spine fracture — so in significant trauma it is preferred over plain radiography.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with a sternal fracture is found to have a concomitant fracture elsewhere that is easily missed. Which structure should be specifically evaluated because it forms a bony ring with the sternum?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Thoracic spine
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The sternum, ribs and thoracic spine form a ring, so a fracture in the sternum should prompt a deliberate search for a concomitant thoracic spine fracture, which is frequently overlooked.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A ventilated trauma patient becomes hypotensive with absent left breath sounds and a deviated trachea. What is the immediate action?
options: Urgent portable chest X-ray before any treatment
Immediate needle/finger decompression of the left chest
Sit the patient up and give furosemide
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Immediate needle/finger decompression of the left chest
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is a tension pneumothorax — a clinical diagnosis. Decompress immediately (needle/finger thoracostomy) BEFORE any imaging; waiting for a chest X-ray can be fatal.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A breathless patient has a CXR showing bat-wing alveolar shadowing, Kerley B lines, cardiomegaly and small bilateral effusions. What is the diagnosis and initial treatment?
options: Heart failure — sit up, oxygen, IV furosemide
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Heart failure — sit up, oxygen, IV furosemide
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The ABCDE pattern (Alveolar oedema, kerley B, Cardiomegaly, Dilated upper-lobe vessels, Effusions) is pulmonary oedema from heart failure. Initial treatment: sit up, oxygen, IV furosemide.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A preterm neonate is grunting with intercostal recession. CXR shows diffuse ground-glass shadowing with air bronchograms and reduced lung volumes. What is the diagnosis and key treatment?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Respiratory distress syndrome — surfactant + CPAP
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Ground-glass reticulogranular shadowing with air bronchograms and low lung volumes in a preterm baby is RDS (surfactant deficiency). Give exogenous surfactant and respiratory support (CPAP/ventilation); antenatal steroids prevent it.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 78-year-old with chronic constipation has a supine AXR showing a large inverted-U ('coffee bean') gas-filled loop arising from the pelvis and projecting towards the right upper quadrant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Sigmoid volvulus
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A coffee-bean/inverted-U loop rising out of the pelvis and pointing to the RUQ is the classic sigmoid volvulus. Caecal volvulus instead displaces the caecum to the LUQ ('embryo'/comma shape). It is the commonest volvulus and typically affects elderly, constipated patients.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with a flare of ulcerative colitis is febrile and tachycardic. The supine AXR shows a transverse colon dilated to 7 cm with mucosal islands and loss of haustra. What is the immediate concern?
options: Toxic megacolon with risk of perforation
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Toxic megacolon with risk of perforation
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A transverse colon >6 cm with mucosal islands/thumbprinting, loss of haustra and systemic toxicity in a colitic patient is toxic megacolon — a medical emergency that risks perforation and needs urgent surgical and gastroenterology review.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A registrar suspects a bowel perforation. Which single investigation is best for demonstrating free intraperitoneal air?
options: Lateral decubitus abdominal film in the dark
Ultrasound of the right upper quadrant
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Erect chest X-ray
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Free intraperitoneal air is best seen as air under the diaphragm on an erect chest X-ray. The supine AXR is poor at demonstrating free air, so it is not the correct film when perforation is suspected (CT is definitive).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On a supine AXR, which feature best identifies a dilated loop as SMALL bowel rather than large bowel?
options: Haustra that do not cross the full lumen
Valvulae conniventes crossing the full width of the lumen
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Valvulae conniventes crossing the full width of the lumen
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Small bowel lies centrally and shows valvulae conniventes — closely spaced lines that cross the ENTIRE width of the lumen. Large bowel is peripheral with haustra that only project partway across. The relevant small-bowel dilatation threshold is >3 cm, not >6 cm.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which statement about calcified structures on a plain AXR is correct?
options: About 90% of renal/ureteric calculi are radio-opaque
Only about 10% of renal calculi are radio-opaque
Vascular calcification never appears on plain films
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: About 90% of renal/ureteric calculi are radio-opaque
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Roughly 90% of renal/ureteric stones are radio-opaque and may be seen on AXR, whereas only about 10% of gallstones are radio-opaque, so a normal AXR does not exclude gallstones. Pancreatic and vascular (e.g. aortic) calcification are also common incidental findings.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 68-year-old with sudden severe epigastric pain and a rigid abdomen is suspected of having a perforated peptic ulcer. Which single plain radiograph is most sensitive for detecting free intraperitoneal gas?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Erect (upright) chest X-ray
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: On an erect CXR free gas rises to sit beneath the diaphragm, giving a thin lucent crescent under the right hemidiaphragm, and even small volumes are detectable. The routine erect AXR adds little and is largely abandoned; CT is used when plain films are equivocal.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An erect abdominal film shows multiple long air-fluid levels in centrally placed dilated loops with valvulae conniventes crossing the full bowel width, while the rectum is empty of gas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Small-bowel obstruction
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Central dilated loops (>3 cm) with valvulae conniventes crossing the full width, multiple air-fluid levels, and a collapsed distal bowel/empty rectum indicate mechanical small-bowel obstruction. Ileus would show generalised gas including the rectum with no transition point.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A supine abdominal film shows the bowel wall outlined by gas on both its luminal and peritoneal sides, making the wall itself clearly visible. What does this represent?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Rigler's (double-wall) sign of pneumoperitoneum
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Rigler's sign is gas on both sides of the bowel wall, seen with free intraperitoneal gas, and indicates a perforated viscus — a surgical emergency requiring resuscitation, IV antibiotics and urgent surgical review, not merely a radiological curiosity.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 34-year-old presents with acute left-sided loin-to-groin colic and microscopic haematuria. What is the single most appropriate first-line imaging investigation?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Non-contrast CT KUB
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: CT KUB is the investigation of choice for acute renal/ureteric colic: it is highly sensitive, detects radiolucent stones, and defines size, site and obstruction. A plain KUB is not first-line for acute diagnosis — its role is follow-up of a known opaque stone.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with recurrent stones has a normal plain KUB despite classic colic. Which stone composition best explains a stone that is invisible on the plain film?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Uric acid
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Uric acid (and indinavir) stones are radiolucent and invisible on KUB, though visible on CT. Calcium oxalate/phosphate and struvite are radio-opaque; cystine is only faintly opaque but still usually visible.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A KUB shows a rounded calcific density in the pelvis with a lucent centre, lying below the ischial spines and off the expected ureteric line. What is this most likely to be?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Phlebolith
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Phleboliths are rounded pelvic venous calcifications, typically smooth with a lucent centre and sited below the ischial spines away from the ureteric course — a classic mimic of a distal ureteric stone, which is usually irregular, dense and on the ureteric line.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with a known obstructing ureteric stone develops a fever of 39°C, rigors and hydronephrosis on imaging. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Discharge with oral antibiotics and follow-up KUB
