Watchful waiting for spontaneous stone passage
Oral analgesia and repeat plain KUB in 48 hours
Urgent decompression (nephrostomy or ureteric stent) plus IV antibiotics
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Urgent decompression (nephrostomy or ureteric stent) plus IV antibiotics
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: An obstructing, infected stone (pyonephrosis) is a urological emergency. It requires urgent drainage of the obstructed, infected system by nephrostomy or stent together with IV antibiotics and resuscitation; definitive stone treatment (e.g. lithotripsy) is deferred.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An 82-year-old woman falls and presents with a shortened, externally rotated left leg. The AP pelvis shows a break in Shenton's line at the femoral neck with the fracture line above the intertrochanteric region. Which classification and typical management is correct?
options: Intracapsular subcapital — high AVN risk, hemiarthroplasty/THR
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Intracapsular subcapital — high AVN risk, hemiarthroplasty/THR
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A fracture at the femoral neck above the trochanters is intracapsular. This disrupts the retinacular blood supply to the femoral head, carrying a high risk of avascular necrosis, so it is typically treated with hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement rather than fixation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A young man is brought in after a motorbike crash. The AP pelvis shows widening of the pubic symphysis to 4 cm and he is hypotensive. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Discharge with analgesia and outpatient follow-up
Perform an isolated CT head before any intervention
Spring the pelvis to confirm instability
Apply a pelvic binder and activate the major haemorrhage protocol
Order an outpatient MRI to look for occult fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Apply a pelvic binder and activate the major haemorrhage protocol
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: An open-book injury with symphyseal diastasis can cause massive retroperitoneal haemorrhage and is life-threatening. A pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters plus resuscitation via the major haemorrhage protocol and urgent trauma/orthopaedic input is required. Springing the pelvis is contraindicated as it can worsen bleeding.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 70-year-old cannot weight-bear on the right hip after a fall. The AP pelvis is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: MRI of the hip to exclude an occult fracture
Repeat the same AP pelvis X-ray in one week
Bone scan only if pain persists for six weeks
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: MRI of the hip to exclude an occult fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A normal radiograph does not exclude a hip fracture. In a patient who cannot weight-bear, an occult fracture must be excluded with MRI (the most sensitive test), as delayed diagnosis increases morbidity and mortality.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An elderly constipated patient has a large ‘coffee-bean’ loop arising from the pelvis on AXR. What is the first-line management?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Flexible sigmoidoscopy and flatus-tube decompression
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A coffee-bean loop from the pelvis is a sigmoid volvulus. First-line management is endoscopic decompression (flexible sigmoidoscopy + flatus tube); recurrent cases need elective sigmoid colectomy. (Caecal volvulus, by contrast, needs surgery.)

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An erect chest X-ray shows free air under the right hemidiaphragm in a patient with peritonitis. What is the appropriate initial management?
options: NBM, IV fluids and urgent surgical review
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: NBM, IV fluids and urgent surgical review
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Free air under the diaphragm indicates a perforated viscus (pneumoperitoneum). Initial management is resuscitation (NBM, IV access/fluids, analgesia, IV antibiotics) and urgent surgical review; CT localises the perforation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A premature neonate has abdominal distension and bloody stools. The AXR shows dilated loops with linear gas in the bowel wall. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Necrotising enterocolitis
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Linear intramural gas (pneumatosis intestinalis) with dilated loops in a preterm baby with feeding intolerance and bloody stool is necrotising enterocolitis. Portal venous gas and free air (Rigler’s/football sign) indicate perforation. Manage with NBM, NG, IV antibiotics and surgery if perforated.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 24-year-old man attends the ED after a rugby tackle with his arm forced into abduction and external rotation. He supports the affected arm and cannot bring it across his chest. An AP shoulder radiograph shows the humeral head lying medial to and below the coracoid process. Which nerve is most at risk and must be documented before reduction?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Axillary nerve
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is a classic anterior (sub-coracoid) dislocation. The axillary nerve is most vulnerable — assess sensation over the "regimental badge" area of the lateral upper arm and deltoid function before and after reduction.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 40-year-old woman is brought in after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure with a painful shoulder held fixed in internal rotation; she cannot externally rotate it. The AP radiograph shows the humeral head appearing rounded and symmetrical ("light bulb" sign) with loss of the normal glenohumeral overlap. What is the most important next step?
options: Discharge with a sling as the AP is essentially normal
Request an urgent MRI of the shoulder
Immediately attempt closed reduction without further imaging
Arrange an outpatient ultrasound of the rotator cuff
Obtain an axial or scapular-Y view to confirm the diagnosis
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Obtain an axial or scapular-Y view to confirm the diagnosis
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The history (seizure) plus the light-bulb sign strongly suggests a posterior dislocation — the classic missed diagnosis. A second orthogonal (axial/Y) view is essential to confirm the head is displaced posteriorly out of the glenoid.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An 82-year-old woman falls onto her outstretched hand and has a painful, swollen shoulder. The radiograph shows a fracture through the surgical neck of the humerus with two displaced parts. Which classification is used to grade this injury?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Neer classification
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Proximal humeral fractures are graded by the Neer classification, which counts the number of displaced parts (head, shaft, greater and lesser tuberosities). Garden is for femoral neck, Weber for ankle, Salter-Harris for physeal, and Gustilo-Anderson for open fractures.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 24-year-old man falls onto his shoulder playing rugby. The X-ray shows a mid-shaft clavicle fracture with the medial fragment elevated. Which muscle is responsible for the upward pull on the medial fragment?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Sternocleidomastoid
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: In middle-third fractures the medial fragment is elevated by the pull of sternocleidomastoid, while the lateral fragment is depressed by the weight of the arm — the classic displacement pattern.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 30-year-old woman has an isolated, minimally displaced middle-third clavicle fracture with intact skin, normal distal pulses and normal neurology. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Immediate open reduction and internal fixation
Urgent CT angiogram of the subclavian vessels
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Broad arm sling and analgesia
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The great majority of uncomplicated middle-third fractures are managed conservatively with a broad arm sling and analgesia, mobilising as pain allows; most unite well. Surgery is reserved for complicated patterns.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 40-year-old man is thrown from a motorbike and sustains a medial-third clavicle fracture. He reports difficulty breathing and there is fullness at the sternoclavicular region. Which complication must be excluded urgently?
options: Posterior displacement compressing the trachea and great vessels
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Posterior displacement compressing the trachea and great vessels
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Medial-third fractures are rare and imply high-energy trauma. Posterior displacement can compress the trachea and mediastinal great vessels — a surgical emergency requiring urgent assessment (often CT) and senior/orthopaedic input.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An 82-year-old woman falls onto her shoulder and a radiograph shows a surgical neck fracture of the humerus. On examination she has weakness of shoulder abduction and reduced sensation over the lateral shoulder. Which nerve is most likely injured?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Axillary nerve
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus and is at risk in surgical neck fractures. Injury causes deltoid weakness (abduction) and 'regimental badge' sensory loss over the lateral shoulder. The radial nerve relates to the mid-shaft, and the median nerve to supracondylar fractures.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 30-year-old man sustains a spiral fracture of the distal third of the humeral shaft. He is subsequently found to have wrist drop and sensory loss over the dorsal first web space. Which fracture eponym and nerve does this describe?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Holstein-Lewis fracture — radial nerve
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A Holstein-Lewis fracture is a spiral fracture of the distal third of the humeral shaft that classically entraps the radial nerve as it pierces the intermuscular septum, causing wrist drop and dorsal first web space sensory loss. The radial nerve runs in the spiral/radial groove of the humerus.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 6-year-old falls on an outstretched hand and has a supracondylar humeral fracture. The hand is cool, pale, and the radial pulse is absent. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Discharge with a broad-arm sling and fracture clinic follow-up
Apply a full circumferential plaster cast and repeat X-ray in 1 week
Reassure and observe as pulses commonly return spontaneously over days
Urgent reduction and orthopaedic input as a surgical emergency
Prescribe analgesia and arrange outpatient MRI
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Urgent reduction and orthopaedic input as a surgical emergency
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A supracondylar fracture with an absent radial pulse and signs of ischaemia threatens the brachial artery and is a surgical emergency. It requires urgent reduction and orthopaedic involvement to restore perfusion and prevent compartment syndrome and Volkmann's ischaemic contracture. Delay or a circumferential cast risks limb-threatening ischaemia.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 45-year-old man falls onto his outstretched hand and cannot fully extend his elbow. The lateral radiograph shows an elevated anterior fat pad and a visible posterior fat pad, but no fracture line. Which fracture is most likely?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Radial head fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: In an adult, a fat pad sign (effusion) with no visible fracture most commonly represents an occult radial head fracture — the commonest occult adult elbow fracture after a FOOSH. It is managed as a fracture: sling and re-image/follow up.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On a paediatric lateral elbow film, the anterior humeral line passes through the anterior third of the capitellum rather than the middle third. What does this suggest?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Posteriorly displaced supracondylar fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The anterior humeral line should pass through the middle third of the capitellum. When it falls anteriorly, the capitellum has displaced posteriorly relative to the humerus — the hallmark of a posteriorly displaced supracondylar fracture.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 6-year-old's elbow film appears to show a trochlear ossification centre but no medial (internal) epicondyle centre. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Normal — the trochlea can ossify first
Avulsed medial epicondyle displaced into the joint
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Avulsed medial epicondyle displaced into the joint
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: By the CRITOE sequence the medial epicondyle must ossify before the trochlea. A 'trochlea' without a preceding medial epicondyle means the medial epicondyle has avulsed and lies within the joint — that fragment is the displaced epicondyle, not the trochlea.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A child with a displaced supracondylar fracture has an absent radial pulse and cannot make the 'OK' sign. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Discharge with a sling and safety-net advice
Urgent orthopaedic referral for assessment of vascular and nerve injury
Reassure and re-image in one week
Apply a full plaster cast and send home
Prescribe analgesia and arrange outpatient physiotherapy
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Urgent orthopaedic referral for assessment of vascular and nerve injury
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A supracondylar fracture can injure the brachial artery and median nerve (classically the anterior interosseous branch — loss of the 'OK' sign). An absent pulse signals vascular compromise, a surgical emergency requiring urgent orthopaedic input, not discharge or delayed follow-up.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with a mid-shaft humeral fracture cannot extend the wrist or fingers. Which nerve is injured and what is the usual management?
options: Radial nerve — splint and expect spontaneous recovery
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Radial nerve — splint and expect spontaneous recovery
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Wrist drop from a mid-shaft humeral fracture is a radial nerve injury (spiral groove). It is usually a neurapraxia that recovers over 2–3 months; manage with a cock-up splint and observe, exploring only if open or no recovery.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 24-year-old falls and an X-ray shows a fracture of the proximal third of the ulna. On the lateral elbow view, a line drawn along the radial neck does not pass through the centre of the capitellum. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Monteggia fracture-dislocation
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A proximal ulnar fracture combined with a disrupted radiocapitellar line (radial head dislocation) defines a Monteggia injury. MUGR: Monteggia = Ulna. In adults this typically requires ORIF.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A distal radial shaft fracture is seen on X-ray. Which additional finding would confirm a Galeazzi fracture-dislocation?
options: Dislocation of the radial head at the elbow
A fracture of the proximal ulna
Buckling of the distal radial cortex only
Widening/dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Widening/dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Galeazzi = distal Radius fracture with DRUJ disruption (MUGR: Galeazzi = Radius). Radial head dislocation and proximal ulnar fracture belong to Monteggia; cortical buckling alone suggests a paediatric buckle fracture.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Six hours after casting a both-bone forearm fracture, a patient reports severe pain that is worse than expected and markedly increased on passive finger extension. Distal pulses are present. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and prescribe stronger oral analgesia
Urgent assessment for compartment syndrome and consideration of fasciotomy
Repeat the X-ray to check alignment
Elevate the limb and review in the morning
Remove the cast and discharge with advice
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Urgent assessment for compartment syndrome and consideration of fasciotomy
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are the earliest signs of compartment syndrome; pulses are often preserved until late. This is a limb-threatening surgical emergency requiring urgent fasciotomy, not reassurance or delay.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 72-year-old woman falls onto an outstretched hand. Radiographs show an extra-articular distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation and a “dinner fork” clinical deformity. Which fracture is this?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Colles' fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Colles' is an extra-articular distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement/angulation producing the dinner-fork deformity, classically after a FOOSH in an osteoporotic elderly woman. Smith's is volar (garden spade); Barton's is intra-articular.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On a lateral wrist radiograph, the lunate is seated normally on the distal radius but the capitate is dislocated dorsally and no longer articulates with the lunate. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Perilunate dislocation
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: In a perilunate dislocation the radius–lunate alignment is preserved but the capitate dislocates (usually dorsally) off the lunate. In a lunate dislocation it is the lunate itself that tips volar off the radius (“spilled teacup”). Both are orthopaedic emergencies.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which set of values represents the approximately normal distal radius parameters used to assess adequacy of reduction?
options: Radial height ~22 mm, inclination ~11°, volar tilt ~5°
Radial height ~5 mm, inclination ~30°, dorsal tilt ~22°
Radial height ~11 mm, inclination ~22°, volar tilt ~11°
Radial height ~30 mm, inclination ~11°, volar tilt ~22°
Radial height ~11 mm, inclination ~11°, dorsal tilt ~11°
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Radial height ~11 mm, inclination ~22°, volar tilt ~11°
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The standard teaching values are radial height ~11 mm, radial inclination ~22° and volar (palmar) tilt ~11°. In Colles' the volar tilt is reversed to dorsal tilt — restoring these parameters is the goal of reduction.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 22-year-old man falls onto his outstretched hand playing football. He has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and pain on axial compression of the thumb. A dedicated scaphoid series is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and discharge with advice that it is a simple sprain
Prescribe analgesia and arrange routine physiotherapy
Request a bone scan in 6 weeks
Apply a full above-elbow cast and review in 3 months
Immobilise in a thumb spica (scaphoid/futuro splint) and arrange repeat imaging in 10–14 days or MRI
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Immobilise in a thumb spica (scaphoid/futuro splint) and arrange repeat imaging in 10–14 days or MRI
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Snuffbox tenderness with a normal initial film represents a frequently occult scaphoid fracture. Treat as a fracture: immobilise and re-image (repeat X-ray at 10–14 days or MRI, which is most sensitive). Discharging as a sprain risks AVN and non-union.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which anatomical feature explains why a proximal pole scaphoid fracture is at high risk of avascular necrosis?
options: The scaphoid has a rich dual arterial supply from the ulnar and radial arteries
The scaphoid has a retrograde blood supply entering the distal pole from the dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery
The scaphoid is entirely covered in periosteum with abundant vessels
The scaphoid receives its blood supply directly from the interosseous membrane
Blood enters at the proximal pole from the anterior interosseous artery
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: The scaphoid has a retrograde blood supply entering the distal pole from the dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery enters at the distal pole and perfuses the bone distal-to-proximal (retrograde). A proximal pole or waist fracture therefore devascularises the proximal fragment, causing AVN and non-union.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which statement about the initial X-ray in suspected scaphoid fracture is correct?
options: A normal scaphoid series reliably excludes a fracture
A single PA wrist view is the definitive investigation
CT is contraindicated because of radiation to the wrist
The fracture is frequently occult (not visible) on the initial film despite a correct scaphoid series
A visible fracture line is required before any immobilisation is applied
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: The fracture is frequently occult (not visible) on the initial film despite a correct scaphoid series
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Scaphoid fractures are often invisible initially; a normal film does not exclude the diagnosis. This is why clinical suspicion (snuffbox tenderness) mandates immobilisation and further imaging (repeat X-ray, MRI, or CT) rather than discharge.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 22-year-old man attends ED after punching a wall. X-ray shows a fracture of the 5th metacarpal neck with volar angulation. On examination his little finger overlaps the ring finger when he makes a fist. What is the most important management priority?
options: Discharge with buddy strapping as angulation is well tolerated
Immediate open reduction and internal fixation of all metacarpal neck fractures
Reassure and review in fracture clinic in 6 weeks with no intervention
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Correction of the rotational deformity
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Volar angulation at the 5th metacarpal neck is often tolerated because of the mobile CMC joint, but rotational malalignment (finger scissoring/overlap on flexion) causes functional impairment and must be corrected. Rotation is a clinical diagnosis, checked by ensuring the fingers point toward the scaphoid on flexion.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 30-year-old presents with pain at the base of the thumb after a fall. X-ray shows an intra-articular fracture at the base of the 1st metacarpal with a small volar-ulnar fragment remaining in place while the shaft is displaced proximally. Which muscle is responsible for the displacement?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Abductor pollicis longus
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is a Bennett's fracture-dislocation. The small volar-ulnar fragment is anchored by the anterior oblique ligament, while abductor pollicis longus pulls the metacarpal shaft proximally and radially, making the injury unstable.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 25-year-old attends ED with a 1 cm laceration over the knuckle of the right hand sustained during a fight. He reports his fist struck the other man's face. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Primary closure with sutures and discharge
Steri-strips and a tetanus booster only
Thorough exploration/washout and antibiotics, left open, with hand referral
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Thorough exploration/washout and antibiotics, left open, with hand referral
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A knuckle wound from a punch is a 'fight bite' (clenched-fist injury) and must be treated as a human-bite wound. It risks septic arthritis and extensor tenosynovitis. It requires washout, antibiotics (e.g. co-amoxiclav), and must never be closed primarily; hand-surgery involvement is standard.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient cannot actively extend the tip of their finger after a ball struck the fingertip. X-ray shows a small avulsion fragment at the dorsal base of the distal phalanx. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Mallet finger
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Mallet finger is a bony avulsion of the extensor tendon at the dorsal base of the distal phalanx, producing a drooped DIP that cannot be actively extended. A dorsal avulsion flake is seen on the lateral view.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A skier falls onto an outstretched hand with a ski pole, forcing the thumb into abduction. There is pain and instability at the thumb MCP joint, and X-ray shows a small avulsion at the base of the proximal phalanx. Which structure is injured?
options: Radial collateral ligament of the thumb MCP
Volar plate of the thumb IP joint
Ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb MCP
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb MCP
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is gamekeeper's/skier's thumb: injury to the ulnar collateral ligament at the thumb MCP joint (± bony avulsion) from forced abduction. It causes MCP instability and, if a displaced Stener lesion is present, requires surgical repair.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An 82-year-old woman falls and presents with a shortened, externally rotated left leg. AP pelvis shows a completely displaced subcapital fracture (Garden IV). What is the most appropriate definitive management?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A displaced intracapsular (Garden III–IV) fracture disrupts the femoral head's blood supply, giving a high risk of AVN and non-union if fixed. The head is therefore replaced — THR in fitter, mobile patients, otherwise hemiarthroplasty. DHS and IM nails are for extracapsular fractures; screws suit undisplaced intracapsular ones.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which statement about intracapsular versus extracapsular neck of femur fractures is correct?
options: Extracapsular fractures carry the highest risk of avascular necrosis
The capsule attaches distal to the lesser trochanter
Subtrochanteric fractures are best treated with a dynamic hip screw
Intracapsular fractures typically disrupt the retrograde supply from the medial femoral circumflex artery
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Intracapsular fractures typically disrupt the retrograde supply from the medial femoral circumflex artery
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Intracapsular (subcapital/transcervical) fractures threaten the retrograde medial femoral circumflex supply, risking AVN. Extracapsular fractures (intertrochanteric, subtrochanteric) spare it. The capsule attaches along the intertrochanteric line; intertrochanteric fractures are extracapsular; subtrochanteric fractures are nailed.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An elderly man cannot weight-bear after a fall; the hip is painful with a shortened, externally rotated leg. Two-view plain films are reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Discharge with analgesia and outpatient follow-up
MRI of the hip to exclude an occult fracture
Repeat plain X-ray in two weeks
Reassure and mobilise as pain allows
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: MRI of the hip to exclude an occult fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A strong clinical picture of NOF fracture with normal radiographs mandates further imaging, as an occult fracture may be invisible on plain film. MRI is the most sensitive (CT is an alternative). Discharging or mobilising the patient risks displacing an undisplaced fracture and causing serious harm.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An 82-year-old woman on 6 years of alendronate presents with a fracture of the proximal femur after standing up. The X-ray shows a transverse subtrochanteric fracture with focal lateral cortical thickening and beaking. She reports weeks of preceding thigh pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Metastatic pathological fracture from breast cancer
Atypical femoral fracture related to bisphosphonate use
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Atypical femoral fracture related to bisphosphonate use
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Transverse subtrochanteric/diaphyseal fracture with lateral cortical beaking, prodromal thigh pain and long-term bisphosphonate use are classic for an atypical femoral fracture; these are frequently bilateral, so the other femur should also be imaged.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 24-year-old man has an isolated closed mid-shaft femoral fracture after a motorbike crash. He is tachycardic and hypotensive with no external bleeding. What is the most important immediate concern?
options: Significant blood loss into the thigh causing hypovolaemic shock
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Significant blood loss into the thigh causing hypovolaemic shock
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A closed femoral shaft fracture can sequester ~1–1.5 L of blood, and with tachycardia and hypotension the priority is resuscitation and assessment for haemorrhagic shock, activating the major haemorrhage protocol if needed.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 30-year-old man is 48 hours post intramedullary nailing of a femoral shaft fracture. He becomes acutely breathless and confused, with a petechial rash over the axillae and conjunctivae. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Fat embolism syndrome
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The triad of respiratory distress, cerebral dysfunction (confusion) and a petechial rash appearing 24–72 hours after a long-bone fracture is characteristic of fat embolism syndrome.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 40-year-old falls from a ladder onto a flexed knee. AP and standard lateral radiographs show no fracture line, but a horizontal-beam lateral shows a straight horizontal interface in the suprapatellar recess. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and discharge with a normal X-ray
CT of the knee to identify an intra-articular fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: CT of the knee to identify an intra-articular fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The fat–fluid level is a lipohaemarthrosis — marrow fat floating on blood indicating an intra-articular fracture (often a subtle tibial plateau fracture) even when no line is seen. It is an intra-articular fracture until proven otherwise, so proceed to CT.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which single finding, if present, mandates a knee radiograph under the Ottawa knee rules?
options: Inability to weight-bear for 4 steps immediately and in the ED
A small effusion with full range of movement
Pain reproduced on resisted hip flexion
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Inability to weight-bear for 4 steps immediately and in the ED
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The Ottawa criteria are age ≥55, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, inability to flex to 90°, or inability to weight-bear 4 steps both immediately and in the ED. Medial joint-line tenderness and an isolated effusion are not criteria.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A young footballer sustains a valgus/rotational injury. The AP film shows a thin vertical sliver of bone avulsed from the lateral margin of the proximal tibia. Which associated injury is most likely?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Anterior cruciate ligament rupture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is a Segond fracture — a cortical avulsion of the lateral tibial condyle that is highly associated with ACL rupture (and frequently meniscal tears). MRI and orthopaedic referral are warranted.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 24-year-old footballer sustains a twisting ankle injury. Radiographs show a medial malleolar fracture and widening of the medial joint space, but no lateral malleolar fracture. He is tender over the upper calf. Which additional injury is most likely?
options: Fracture of the proximal fibula (Maisonneuve fracture)
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Fracture of the proximal fibula (Maisonneuve fracture)
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Medial malleolar/deltoid injury with syndesmotic disruption and proximal calf tenderness suggests a Maisonneuve fracture. The force travels up through the interosseous membrane to exit at the proximal fibula, which must be examined and imaged.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 30-year-old has a closed mid-shaft tibial fracture. Six hours later he has severe pain requiring escalating opioids and agonising pain when his toes are passively extended. His foot pulses remain palpable. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and continue analgesia as pulses are present
Elevate the limb above heart level and re-examine in the morning
Apply a tighter cast to stabilise the fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Urgent surgical fasciotomy
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are early signs of acute compartment syndrome, for which the tibia is the classic site. A palpable pulse does not exclude it. It is a surgical emergency requiring urgent fasciotomy.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which feature of the tibia best explains its high rate of open fractures?
options: It has a rich muscular envelope on all sides
It is the shortest of the long bones
It has a dual blood supply making it fragile
It ossifies later than other long bones
Its anteromedial border is subcutaneous with thin overlying skin
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Its anteromedial border is subcutaneous with thin overlying skin
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The anteromedial (subcutaneous) surface of the tibia lies directly beneath thin skin with little muscle protection, so displaced fragments readily breach the skin, producing open fractures and poor soft-tissue coverage.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 30-year-old inverts her ankle. She has tenderness over the tip of the lateral malleolus and cannot walk 4 steps in the ED. According to the Ottawa Ankle Rules, what is the appropriate action?
options: No imaging; it is a simple sprain
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: X-ray the ankle
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Malleolar-zone pain plus bony tenderness at the lateral malleolus tip AND inability to weight-bear both meet the Ottawa criteria, so a plain ankle X-ray is indicated. MRI/CT are not first-line, and foot films are for the Ottawa foot rules.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An ankle radiograph shows a fibular fracture ABOVE the level of the syndesmosis. How is this classified and what does it imply?
options: Weber C — syndesmosis disrupted, unstable, often surgical
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Weber C — syndesmosis disrupted, unstable, often surgical
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A fibular fracture above the syndesmosis is Weber C, which implies the syndesmosis is disrupted, making the ankle unstable and usually requiring operative fixation. Weber A is below and B is at the level of the syndesmosis.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient has medial ankle tenderness and a widened medial clear space on the mortise view, but no lateral malleolus fracture is seen on the ankle films. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: X-ray the whole leg to look for a proximal fibula fracture
Discharge with a diagnosis of ankle sprain
Reassure and repeat the ankle film in 2 weeks
Apply a below-knee cast and discharge
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: X-ray the whole leg to look for a proximal fibula fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This pattern suggests a Maisonneuve injury — a proximal fibula fracture with syndesmotic disruption. The whole leg must be imaged because the fracture lies outside the standard ankle field, and the injury is unstable.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 22-year-old rolls his ankle playing football and has tenderness over the base of the 5th metatarsal. X-ray shows a fracture at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction, about 1.8 cm distal to the tip of the tuberosity. Which statement is correct?
options: This is a pseudo-Jones avulsion fracture that will heal quickly in comfortable footwear
The fracture is caused by traction from the tibialis posterior tendon
This is a true Jones fracture in a watershed blood-supply zone with a higher risk of non-union
It should always be managed by immediate full weight-bearing mobilisation
The location is irrelevant to prognosis at the 5th metatarsal base
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: This is a true Jones fracture in a watershed blood-supply zone with a higher risk of non-union
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A fracture at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction (roughly 1.5–2 cm distal to the tuberosity tip) is a true Jones fracture. This region has a relatively poor (watershed) blood supply, giving a higher rate of delayed and non-union, so it is often managed non-weight-bearing with fixation considered in athletes. An avulsion of the very proximal tuberosity (peroneus brevis pull) is the benign pseudo-Jones.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient has midfoot pain after a fall. Which single radiographic feature should most strongly prompt weight-bearing views or CT to exclude a Lisfranc injury?
options: A smooth bipartite sesamoid beneath the 1st metatarsal head
Periosteal callus along the 2nd metatarsal shaft
A transverse fracture at the tip of the 5th metatarsal tuberosity
A 'fleck sign' avulsion fragment in the interval between the medial cuneiform and 2nd metatarsal base
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: A 'fleck sign' avulsion fragment in the interval between the medial cuneiform and 2nd metatarsal base
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The fleck sign represents an avulsion at the Lisfranc ligament and is a key clue to a tarsometatarsal fracture-dislocation. Combined with malalignment of the 2nd metatarsal base and the middle cuneiform, or widening of the 1st–2nd metatarsal gap, it warrants weight-bearing views or CT because Lisfranc injuries are easily missed and carry high morbidity.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Under the Ottawa foot rules, which finding is an indication to obtain a foot radiograph in a patient with midfoot pain?
options: Bony tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Bony tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The Ottawa foot rules indicate a foot X-ray if there is midfoot pain plus bony tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal or the navicular, or an inability to weight-bear four steps. Malleolar tenderness relates to the Ottawa ankle (not foot) rules, and calf or Achilles tenderness are not part of the criteria.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 34-year-old roofer falls 4 metres onto his heels. Lateral calcaneal radiograph shows Böhler's angle reduced to 12°. What does this most strongly indicate?
options: A normal variant of no significance
An avulsion of the Achilles insertion only
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: A depressed intra-articular calcaneal fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Böhler's angle normally measures 20–40°. Flattening to <20° reflects collapse of the posterior facet, the hallmark of a depressed intra-articular fracture — the single most testable sign on the lateral view.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: After confirming a unilateral calcaneal fracture from a fall from height, which associated injury is most important to actively exclude?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Thoracolumbar vertebral fracture
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Around 10% of calcaneal fractures have an associated spinal fracture because the axial load is transmitted up the skeleton. Examining and imaging the thoracolumbar spine (and the opposite heel and pelvis) is essential.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which radiographic view is used to assess Böhler's angle in a suspected calcaneal fracture?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Lateral view
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Böhler's angle is constructed on the lateral radiograph. The axial (Harris) view complements it by showing heel width and tuberosity alignment, but the angle itself is measured on the lateral.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 4-month-old who cannot yet crawl has a spiral femoral shaft fracture. What is the priority?
options: Apply a cast and discharge home
Reassure — femoral fractures are common at this age
Start calcium and vitamin D only
Consider non-accidental injury and make a safeguarding referral
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Consider non-accidental injury and make a safeguarding referral
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A femoral shaft fracture in a non-ambulant infant is a classic red flag for non-accidental injury. It warrants admission, a safeguarding referral, a skeletal survey and senior/paediatric involvement — not discharge.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 68-year-old man has progressive dysphagia to solids and weight loss. Barium swallow shows an irregular narrowing of the mid-oesophagus with abrupt shouldered margins. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and repeat the barium swallow in 6 months
Start a proton pump inhibitor and review
Refer for upper GI endoscopy and biopsy
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Refer for upper GI endoscopy and biopsy
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: An irregular, shouldered stricture with mucosal destruction is malignant until proven otherwise, especially with red-flag features (weight loss, progressive dysphagia). Tissue diagnosis via endoscopic biopsy is required; a smooth tapered stricture would instead suggest a benign peptic cause.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with suspected oesophageal perforation following endoscopy is booked for a contrast swallow. Which contrast agent is most appropriate?
options: Ionic water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) regardless of airway status
No contrast — proceed straight to dilatation
Effervescent granules alone for double contrast
Water-soluble contrast, choosing non-ionic if aspiration is also a risk
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Water-soluble contrast, choosing non-ionic if aspiration is also a risk
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Barium is contraindicated when perforation is suspected as extravasated barium causes severe mediastinitis. Water-soluble contrast is used; however ionic Gastrografin causes pulmonary oedema if aspirated, so a non-ionic iso-osmolar agent is chosen when aspiration is also a concern.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 55-year-old woman reports dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis and a gurgling neck. Barium swallow shows a posterior outpouching that fills with contrast. Which complication of blind NG tube insertion should you be most wary of?
options: Perforation of the pouch by the tube
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Perforation of the pouch by the tube
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: This is a pharyngeal (Zenker's) diverticulum. A blindly passed NG tube can enter the pouch and perforate it, so placement should be under direct vision or fluoroscopic/endoscopic guidance.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 68-year-old man who cannot tolerate endoscopy has a double-contrast barium meal. A gastric ulcer crater is seen projecting beyond the expected line of the gastric wall, with smooth mucosal folds radiating symmetrically to its edge. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Features are diagnostic of malignancy and warrant urgent surgery
This is a Carman meniscus sign indicating carcinoma
The appearances confirm a benign ulcer and no further investigation is needed
Features are typical of a benign ulcer, but endoscopic biopsy is still required to exclude malignancy
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Features are typical of a benign ulcer, but endoscopic biopsy is still required to exclude malignancy
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A crater projecting beyond the lumen with symmetrical radiating folds favours a benign ulcer. However, barium appearances can never confirm benignity — gastric ulcers require endoscopic biopsy to exclude malignancy, which is a key reason endoscopy is now first-line.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient presents with sudden severe epigastric pain and suspected perforated peptic ulcer, but a contrast study of the upper GI tract is requested. Which contrast agent is most appropriate?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin)
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: When perforation is suspected, barium must be avoided because extravasation into the peritoneum causes severe chemical (barium) peritonitis. Water-soluble Gastrografin is used instead as it is safely reabsorbed. (Conversely, Gastrografin is avoided when aspiration risk is high, as it causes pulmonary oedema.)

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: IV Buscopan (hyoscine butylbromide) is routinely given during a barium meal. In which patient is it most clearly contraindicated?
options: A patient with untreated angle-closure glaucoma
A patient with mild iron-deficiency anaemia
A patient with a previous appendicectomy
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: A patient with untreated angle-closure glaucoma
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Buscopan is an antimuscarinic that reduces peristalsis for a still, distended stomach, but its anticholinergic effects contraindicate it in untreated angle-closure glaucoma and warrant caution in significant cardiac disease and prostatic outflow obstruction (risk of acute urinary retention).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 24-year-old with chronic diarrhoea and right iliac fossa pain has a barium follow-through showing a thin ribbon of contrast through a narrowed terminal ileum with skip lesions elsewhere. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Crohn's disease
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The string sign of Kantor (ribbon of barium through a strictured terminal ileum) together with skip lesions is characteristic of Crohn's disease. Ulcerative colitis is a continuous colonic disease and does not cause these small bowel signs; coeliac disease causes fold/malabsorption changes rather than strictures.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with suspected bowel perforation needs a contrast study of the bowel. Which contrast agent is most appropriate?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Water-soluble iodinated contrast (Gastrografin)
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: If perforation or leak is suspected, barium is contraindicated because extravasation causes severe granulomatous (barium) peritonitis. A water-soluble iodinated agent is safely resorbed and is used instead. Gadolinium is an IV MRI agent, not a luminal contrast.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which feature is assessed on the compression spot views of the terminal ileum during a follow-through and is the key target region?
options: Terminal ileal strictures, ulceration and cobblestoning
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Terminal ileal strictures, ulceration and cobblestoning
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Compression (spot) views separate overlapping loops so the terminal ileum — the commonest site of Crohn's and the study's key target — can be assessed for strictures, ulceration, cobblestoning and separation of loops. The stomach, oesophagus, colon and biliary tree are not the focus of the follow-through.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 60-year-old man develops severe chest pain and surgical emphysema after a difficult upper GI endoscopy. Oesophageal perforation is suspected and a contrast swallow is requested. Which contrast agent is most appropriate?
options: Barium sulphate for best mucosal detail
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Low-osmolar non-ionic iodinated contrast
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A leak is suspected, so barium is contraindicated (mediastinitis). This unwell post-instrumentation patient also carries aspiration risk; gastrografin could cause pulmonary oedema if aspirated. Low-osmolar non-ionic contrast is safe both in the mediastinum and in the airway, making it the compromise agent.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: What is the principal hazard of giving ionic hyperosmolar water-soluble contrast (gastrografin) to a patient at risk of aspiration?
options: Acute pulmonary oedema and chemical pneumonitis
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Acute pulmonary oedema and chemical pneumonitis
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The high osmolarity of gastrografin draws fluid into the alveoli if aspirated, causing acute pulmonary oedema and chemical pneumonitis. This is why a low-osmolar non-ionic agent is preferred whenever aspiration risk is present.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient who is 5 days post-oesophagectomy is being assessed before starting oral feeding. What is the water-soluble contrast swallow primarily looking for?
options: Mucosal detail of a suspected malignancy
Contrast extravasation indicating an anastomotic leak
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Contrast extravasation indicating an anastomotic leak
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Post-operative swallows assess anastomotic integrity. The key finding is contrast escaping the lumen (extravasation) at the anastomosis, which signals a leak and would delay feeding. Barium is avoided because a leak is exactly what is being excluded.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient recovering from a stroke undergoes videofluoroscopy. Contrast is seen entering the laryngeal vestibule but remaining above the level of the vocal cords, and the patient does not cough. How is this best described?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Laryngeal penetration
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Contrast in the laryngeal vestibule but ABOVE the vocal cords is penetration. Aspiration requires contrast to pass BELOW the cords into the trachea. Silent aspiration specifically means below-cord contrast with no cough, which has not occurred here.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which feature is the single strongest reason to arrange a videofluoroscopy rather than rely on a bedside swallow assessment?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Identification of silent aspiration
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Silent aspiration (below-cord aspiration with no cough) is invisible on a bedside assessment because there is no clinical warning sign. VFSS visualises it directly, guiding safe feeding decisions.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Regarding contrast choice and safety in videofluoroscopy, which statement is correct?
options: High-osmolar agents are avoided as aspiration can cause pulmonary oedema
High-osmolar water-soluble contrast (e.g. gastrografin) is preferred because aspiration is harmless
Barium is dangerous even in trace amounts and is never used for swallow studies
It is an anatomical rather than functional study
The study delivers no radiation dose
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: High-osmolar agents are avoided as aspiration can cause pulmonary oedema
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: High-osmolar water-soluble agents (gastrografin) draw fluid into the lungs and cause pulmonary oedema if aspirated, so they are avoided when aspiration is likely; low/iso-osmolar agents or barium are used instead. VFSS is a functional study that does involve ionising radiation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with severe chest pain after vomiting is suspected of having an oesophageal perforation but also has a reduced conscious level and aspiration risk. Which contrast agent should be used for the swallow study?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: A low-osmolar non-ionic iodinated agent
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Perforation contraindicates barium (chemical mediastinitis). Standard Gastrografin (hyperosmolar) is dangerous if aspirated (pulmonary oedema). When BOTH perforation and aspiration risk coexist, use a low-osmolar non-ionic iodinated agent, which is safe if it leaks into the mediastinum AND if aspirated.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A barium swallow shows a dilated oesophageal body tapering to a smooth bird-beak at the gastro-oesophageal junction. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start a proton pump inhibitor and reassess in 6 weeks
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Oesophageal manometry and endoscopy
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The bird-beak sign suggests achalasia, but barium is not confirmatory. Manometry is the diagnostic gold standard (aperistalsis + failed LOS relaxation) and endoscopy is needed to exclude a GOJ tumour (pseudoachalasia) before definitive treatment (dilatation, Heller myotomy/POEM).

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: In small bowel enema (enteroclysis), what is the purpose of infusing methylcellulose after the barium?
options: To neutralise gastric acid before contrast reaches the small bowel
To provide a water-soluble alternative in case of perforation
To distend the loops and create a double-contrast effect for superior mucosal detail
To speed transit so the terminal ileum opacifies faster on follow-through
To act as an antispasmodic reducing bowel peristalsis
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: To distend the loops and create a double-contrast effect for superior mucosal detail
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Barium coats the mucosa first; the low-density methylcellulose column is then infused to push the barium onward and actively distend the loops. This double-contrast technique holds the bowel open and reveals subtle strictures and fold abnormalities that would collapse on a single-contrast study.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient is being investigated for suspected low-grade small bowel obstruction. Which statement best reflects the role of enteroclysis in current UK practice?
options: It is the first-line investigation for all small bowel pathology
It has been completely abandoned and is no longer performed
It is preferred over cross-sectional imaging because it avoids ionising radiation
It is only used to assess the colon and rectum
It is a second-line, problem-solving study, as MR and CT enterography are now often preferred
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: It is a second-line, problem-solving study, as MR and CT enterography are now often preferred
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: MR enterography (no radiation, excellent wall and extramural detail) and CT enterography have largely displaced enteroclysis. It remains a dedicated high-detail mucosal study used when cross-sectional imaging is equivocal, e.g. subtle obstruction, Crohn's extent, or obscure GI bleeding.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Why is the tip of the naso-jejunal tube positioned beyond the duodeno-jejunal flexure in enteroclysis?
options: To allow biopsy of the terminal ileum through the tube
To bypass the stomach and pylorus so infusion rate is controlled directly by the radiologist
To reduce the radiation dose delivered to the pelvis
To prevent reflux of colonic contents into the small bowel
To ensure barium is diluted by gastric secretions before imaging
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: To bypass the stomach and pylorus so infusion rate is controlled directly by the radiologist
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Placing the tip past the DJ flexure means contrast delivery no longer depends on gastric emptying. The radiologist can infuse barium and then methylcellulose at a controlled rate, achieving the rapid, controlled distension that gives enteroclysis its superior detail over the oral follow-through.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 74-year-old man has a single-contrast water-soluble enema for suspected large bowel obstruction. Contrast passes freely through the entire colon to a markedly dilated caecum with no transition point. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome)
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Free flow of contrast to a dilated caecum with no mechanical transition point indicates pseudo-obstruction rather than mechanical obstruction. This changes management from surgery towards conservative/decompressive treatment, which is precisely why the water-soluble enema is requested acutely.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with acute severe ulcerative colitis and abdominal distension is suspected of having toxic megacolon. Which imaging investigation is CONTRAINDICATED?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Double-contrast barium enema
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Barium enema is contraindicated in toxic megacolon and where perforation is suspected because the inflamed, thinned colon may perforate, and extravasated barium causes severe chemical peritonitis. If a contrast study is needed, a water-soluble agent is used; plain film and CT are appropriate.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: During a double-contrast barium enema, which medication is given intravenously to reduce colonic spasm and improve image quality?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan)
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: IV hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan) is an antispasmodic that relaxes smooth muscle, reducing spasm and improving distension and mucosal coating. Consent should cover its side effects (blurred vision, dry mouth, urinary retention); it is avoided in angle-closure glaucoma.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 52-year-old woman reports chronic straining and a sensation of incomplete rectal emptying, relieved by vaginal digitation. Defecating proctography shows anterior bulging of the rectal wall with contrast retained in the bulge after evacuation. What is the most likely finding?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Rectocele
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Anterior rectal wall bulging with trapping of contrast and incomplete emptying, classically relieved by digitation, is the hallmark of a rectocele. An enterocele involves small-bowel descent into the rectovaginal space; anismus is a non-relaxing pelvic floor with a failure of the anorectal angle to open.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: During the straining/evacuation phase of a proctogram, the anorectal angle fails to open and remains acute, with markedly prolonged and incomplete evacuation. Which diagnosis does this best represent?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Anismus (paradoxical puborectalis contraction)
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Normally the puborectalis relaxes on straining so the anorectal angle widens to allow evacuation. Failure of the angle to open — a non-relaxing pelvic floor — is anismus, a functional cause of obstructed defecation, distinct from mechanical causes such as a rectocele or intussusception.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which statement about defecating proctography is most accurate?
options: It uses thin water-soluble contrast to assess mucosal detail
It is a static study best interpreted from a single evacuation frame
It carries no radiation dose and is safe to repeat freely in young women
It is a dynamic functional study using thick barium paste with the patient seated on a radiolucent commode
Its main role is to exclude colorectal malignancy
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: It is a dynamic functional study using thick barium paste with the patient seated on a radiolucent commode
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Proctography uses stool-consistency barium paste and lateral fluoroscopy through rest, squeeze, cough and evacuation phases — a dynamic functional assessment of the pelvic floor. It does deliver a pelvic/gonadal radiation dose (hence MR defecography as a radiation-free alternative), and it assesses function rather than screening for malignancy.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 30-year-old woman is being investigated for primary subfertility. At which point in the menstrual cycle is a hysterosalpingogram best performed?
options: The follicular phase, after menses and before ovulation (days ~7-10)
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: The follicular phase, after menses and before ovulation (days ~7-10)
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: HSG is timed to the follicular phase so that an early pregnancy is not irradiated (conception has not yet occurred in that cycle) and the thin endometrium gives a clear cavity view. Menstruation risks intravasation of blood/clot and infection, and later phases risk irradiating an early pregnancy.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An HSG shows contrast filling the right tube with free peritoneal spill, but the left tube is dilated and contrast-filled with no spill from its fimbrial end. What is the left-sided finding?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Distal tubal block with hydrosalpinx
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A dilated, contrast-filled tube that fails to spill at the fimbrial end indicates a distal block with hydrosalpinx, typically post-infective. A cornual block would stop contrast at the uterine end before the tube fills; the uterine findings listed (arcuate, fibroid, Asherman's) are cavity abnormalities, not tubal.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which of the following is the most important step to reduce the risk of pelvic infection when arranging an HSG?
options: Give a large fluid bolus immediately before the study
Screen for and treat chlamydia, and consider prophylactic antibiotics
Use barium rather than water-soluble contrast
Administer a benzodiazepine before the procedure
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Screen for and treat chlamydia, and consider prophylactic antibiotics
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: HSG can flush organisms into the tubes and precipitate a flare of pelvic inflammatory disease, so pre-procedure screening/treatment for chlamydia and consideration of prophylactic antibiotics is key. Barium is never used within the uterine cavity, menstruation is avoided, and fluids/benzodiazepines do not address infection risk.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 6-week-old boy is investigated after antenatal hydronephrosis. MCUG shows a dilated posterior urethra with an abrupt distal calibre change and a thick-walled, trabeculated bladder. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Posterior urethral valves
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A dilated posterior urethra with the 'keyhole' sign and a trabeculated, thick-walled bladder in a boy is characteristic of posterior urethral valves — an important surgical cause of bladder outlet obstruction in neonatal boys.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On MCUG, contrast refluxes up a grossly dilated, tortuous ureter with clubbing of the calyces. What grade of vesicoureteric reflux is this?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Grade V
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Grade V reflux is defined by gross dilatation and tortuosity of the ureter with clubbed calyces and loss of papillary impressions — the most severe grade.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which statement about MCUG safety and technique is correct?
options: Barium sulphate is the contrast of choice
It requires no consent as it is a routine test
Direct radionuclide cystography is a lower-dose alternative for reflux follow-up
Imaging during bladder filling alone is sufficient
It reliably demonstrates renal cortical scarring
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Direct radionuclide cystography is a lower-dose alternative for reflux follow-up
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Water-soluble (not barium) contrast is used, parental consent is required, and the voiding phase is essential. MCUG shows anatomy and reflux but not scarring (DMSA does). For follow-up of known reflux, direct radionuclide cystography delivers a lower gonadal radiation dose.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A 28-year-old man is brought in after a pelvic-crush injury. There is blood at the urethral meatus, a perineal haematoma, and he cannot pass urine. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Insert a urethral Foley catheter and inflate the balloon
Give oral barium and screen the pelvis
Arrange an urgent MRI of the pelvis
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Perform a retrograde urethrogram
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Blood at the meatus with inability to void after pelvic trauma signals urethral injury. A retrograde urethrogram must precede catheterisation, because blind catheter passage can convert a partial urethral tear into a complete one. Cystography and catheterisation follow only once urethral integrity is confirmed.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A cystogram in a trauma patient shows contrast tracking around bowel loops and into the paracolic gutters. Which type of bladder rupture is this, and how is it usually managed?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Intraperitoneal rupture — surgical repair
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Contrast outlining bowel loops and pooling in the paracolic gutters/pouch of Douglas indicates an intraperitoneal rupture (typically a dome tear), which requires operative repair. Extraperitoneal rupture instead shows flame-shaped contrast confined to the perivesical soft tissues and is usually managed conservatively with catheter drainage.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which statement about contrast choice and technique in lower urinary tract fluoroscopy is correct?
options: Barium is preferred because it gives better mucosal detail
The retrograde urethrogram is best performed in a strict AP position
Cystography should always follow catheterisation regardless of suspected urethral injury
Water-soluble contrast is used, and a post-drainage film aids detection of extraperitoneal leaks
Radiation and consent are not relevant considerations for these studies
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Water-soluble contrast is used, and a post-drainage film aids detection of extraperitoneal leaks
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Only water-soluble contrast is used in the urinary tract — extravasated barium causes severe granulomatous reaction. The RUG is performed in an oblique position to project the urethra clear of the bones, catheterisation must not precede a urethrogram when urethral injury is suspected, and radiation/consent/asepsis all apply. The post-drainage film is key for catching subtle extraperitoneal bladder leaks.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient has a unilateral hydronephrosis of unclear cause. Cystoscopic retrograde ureteric cannulation has failed. Which study best opacifies the collecting system and defines the level of obstruction?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Antegrade pyelogram
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: When the retrograde route fails, contrast can be injected antegradely (via percutaneous needle or nephrostomy) to opacify the pelvicalyceal system from above and demonstrate the level and cause of obstruction.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which contrast agent is appropriate for a nephrostogram / antegrade pyelogram?
options: Air as a negative contrast agent
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Water-soluble iodinated contrast
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Water-soluble iodinated contrast is used. Barium is never introduced into the urinary tract; it is a bowel agent and would be harmful if it extravasated or leaked from the collecting system.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Before removing a nephrostomy tube that was placed to relieve an obstructing ureteric stone (now treated), what does a nephrostogram primarily need to confirm?
options: That the renal cortex enhances symmetrically
That the bladder wall is not trabeculated
That the renal artery is patent
That the ureter now drains contrast freely to the bladder
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: That the ureter now drains contrast freely to the bladder
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The key question before removing/capping a nephrostomy is whether the obstruction has resolved and contrast passes freely down the ureter to the bladder. Free antegrade drainage confirms the tube is no longer needed.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A newborn boy has a poor urinary stream and a palpable bladder. MCUG shows a dilated posterior urethra with a ‘keyhole’ appearance. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Posterior urethral valves
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The keyhole sign (dilated posterior urethra ballooning above an obstructed bladder neck) on MCUG in a boy is classic for posterior urethral valves, the commonest cause of bladder outflow obstruction in male infants. Management: catheter, monitor renal function, urgent paediatric urology for valve ablation.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A cystogram in a trauma patient shows contrast outlining loops of bowel and tracking into the paracolic gutters. What does this indicate and what is the management?
options: Extraperitoneal bladder rupture — catheter drainage alone
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Intraperitoneal bladder rupture — surgical repair
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Contrast outlining bowel loops indicates intraperitoneal bladder rupture (usually a dome injury), which requires surgical repair. Extraperitoneal rupture gives flame-shaped contrast confined to the pelvis and is usually managed with catheter drainage.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: During subfertility work-up an HSG shows a dilated left tube with no peritoneal spill on that side and free spill on the right. What is the left-sided finding?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Hydrosalpinx (distal tubal block)
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A dilated tube that fails to spill contrast into the peritoneum is a hydrosalpinx (distal tubal occlusion), usually post-infective. Free spill on the right confirms that side is patent. A hydrosalpinx reduces IVF success and is often removed/clipped before IVF.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A man has blood at the urethral meatus after a pelvic fracture. A retrograde urethrogram shows contrast extravasation at the membranous urethra. What is the correct next step?
options: Pass a urethral catheter to drain the bladder
Insert a suprapubic catheter and refer to urology
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Insert a suprapubic catheter and refer to urology
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Urethral disruption is confirmed. A urethral catheter must NOT be attempted (risk of converting a partial to a complete tear). Establish drainage with a suprapubic catheter and refer to urology. The retrograde urethrogram is the correct first investigation for suspected urethral injury.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient has a persistent discharging tract at a previous laparotomy scar. During a fistulogram, which contrast agent should be used?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Water-soluble iodinated contrast
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Water-soluble iodinated contrast is used because barium tracking into soft tissue or the peritoneal cavity is retained permanently and causes granulomatous reaction or barium peritonitis. Gadolinium is an MRI agent, and air is not used to opacify a tract.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: During a fistulogram, injected contrast opacifies loops of small bowel. What is the most important immediate clinical concern?
options: Fluid and electrolyte loss from a high-output enterocutaneous fistula
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Fluid and electrolyte loss from a high-output enterocutaneous fistula
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Opacification of bowel confirms an enterocutaneous fistula. These can be high-output, causing significant fluid, electrolyte and nutritional losses, which dominate early management alongside skin protection and treating the underlying cause.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which investigation is now preferred over fluoroscopic fistulography for characterising a perianal fistula?
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: MRI pelvis
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: MRI is superior for perianal fistula: it demonstrates the tract in relation to the anal sphincter complex, allows Parks classification, and avoids ionising radiation and catheterisation of the tract.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with recurrent shoulder instability is booked for an MR arthrogram. Immediately after positioning the needle, what does the radiologist inject FIRST under fluoroscopy?
options: A small test dose of iodinated contrast
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: A small test dose of iodinated contrast
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A small bolus of iodinated contrast is injected first to confirm intra-articular position (contrast should flow along the joint recesses). Only once position is confirmed is the dilute gadolinium injected. Barium is never used in joints, and neat gadolinium causes signal loss.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which finding on shoulder arthrography most specifically indicates a full-thickness rotator cuff tear?
options: Contrast leaking into the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa
Reduced joint volume with resistance to injection
Smooth contrast outlining the axillary recess
Contrast filling only the biceps tendon sheath
Pooling of contrast in the deltoid muscle
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Contrast leaking into the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Normally the joint and the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa do not communicate. Contrast tracking through a cuff defect into that bursa indicates a full-thickness tear. Reduced volume suggests adhesive capsulitis, and deltoid pooling indicates an extra-articular (failed) injection.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which is an absolute contraindication to performing joint arthrography?
options: Overlying cellulitis at the puncture site
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Overlying cellulitis at the puncture site
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Passing a needle through infected overlying skin risks seeding the joint and causing septic arthritis, so overlying infection is a contraindication. Prior surgery, osteoarthritis, a suspected labral tear and older age are not contraindications and are often the very reasons for the study.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient underwent open common bile duct exploration and has a T-tube in situ. On day 8 a cholangiogram is planned before tube removal. What is the primary purpose of this study?
options: To dilate a biliary stricture therapeutically
To assess gallbladder contractility after a fatty meal
To confirm the ducts are clear of retained stones and contrast flows freely into the duodenum
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: To confirm the ducts are clear of retained stones and contrast flows freely into the duodenum
