investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The T-tube cholangiogram documents a stone-free biliary tree with free duodenal drainage before the tube is safely removed; it is a diagnostic check, not a therapeutic or pressure study.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which of the following is the most important safety measure when injecting contrast during a T-tube cholangiogram?
options: Inject rapidly under high pressure to opacify the intra-hepatic ducts fully
Inject gently at low pressure with strict asepsis and antibiotic cover
Use barium sulphate for superior mucosal coating
Withhold consent to save time before tube removal
Warm the contrast to body temperature to prevent duct spasm
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Inject gently at low pressure with strict asepsis and antibiotic cover
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: High-pressure injection into an obstructed or infected biliary system causes biliary-venous reflux and can precipitate cholangitis and septicaemia. Gentle low-pressure injection, asepsis and antibiotic cover mitigate this; water-soluble (not barium) contrast is used.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A T-tube cholangiogram shows a rounded filling defect in the distal CBD with no contrast entering the duodenum. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Remove the T-tube immediately as planned
Switch to barium and repeat the study
Discharge the patient with no further imaging
Leave the T-tube in situ and clear the stone, e.g. by ERCP or via the mature tract later
Clamp the tube and remove it the same day regardless
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Leave the T-tube in situ and clear the stone, e.g. by ERCP or via the mature tract later
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A filling defect with obstructed flow indicates a retained stone. The tube is kept in situ to preserve access and drainage; the stone is cleared by ERCP or percutaneous extraction through the mature T-tube tract (around 6 weeks). Note air bubbles can mimic stones, so flushing air from the line first is essential.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A ward nurse cannot obtain any aspirate from a newly placed nasogastric tube in a patient on omeprazole. What is the most appropriate next step before commencing feed?
options: Obtain a chest radiograph and have it interpreted by a competent practitioner before use
Perform the whoosh test by auscultating over the epigastrium while injecting air
Commence feeding as the tube passed easily and the patient is comfortable
Inject barium down the tube and screen under fluoroscopy
Advance the tube 10 cm further and start feed immediately
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Obtain a chest radiograph and have it interpreted by a competent practitioner before use
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: When no aspirate is obtained (or pH is >5.5, common with acid suppression), a CXR is the required second-line check and must be correctly interpreted before the tube is used. The whoosh test is unsafe and abandoned; feeding without confirmation risks a fatal Never Event; barium is never used for this.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: On a chest radiograph, which single feature most strongly indicates a correctly positioned nasogastric tube?
options: The tube deviates to the right and follows a bronchus
The tip lies at the level of the carina in the midline
The tube bisects the carina and its tip lies below the left hemidiaphragm
The tube coils in the mid-oesophagus above the carina
The tip sits at the cavoatrial junction
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: The tube bisects the carina and its tip lies below the left hemidiaphragm
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A correctly sited NG tube follows the midline oesophagus, bisects the carina and passes below the left hemidiaphragm into the stomach. A tube following a bronchus is in the airway; a tip at the carina is too high; the cavoatrial junction is the target for central venous lines, not NG tubes.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient's PICC line flushes but cannot be aspirated. A linogram shows contrast sleeving back over the catheter tip on injection. What is the most likely cause?
options: Correctly functioning line requiring no action
Tip malposition in the right atrium
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Fibrin sheath around the catheter
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: A line that flushes but won't aspirate, with contrast sleeving back over the tip on injection, is the classic appearance of a fibrin sheath. This can allow infused drugs to track back along the catheter towards the skin. The linogram distinguishes this from frank extravasation, kinking or malposition.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: A patient with a cardiac pacemaker needs imaging of a suspected lumbar nerve-root compression. MRI is contraindicated. During CT myelography, which contrast agent is appropriate to inject?
options: Non-ionic low-osmolar contrast licensed for intrathecal use (e.g. iohexol)
Gadolinium-based contrast at standard IV dose
Normal saline with a dilute ionic contrast
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Non-ionic low-osmolar contrast licensed for intrathecal use (e.g. iohexol)
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Only a non-ionic, low-osmolar agent specifically licensed for intrathecal use (e.g. iohexol) may be injected into the subarachnoid space. Ionic contrast such as gastrografin injected intrathecally causes fatal neurotoxicity, seizures and ascending myeloencephalopathy. Barium is for the GI lumen only, and gadolinium is not the standard intrathecal myelographic agent.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Which of the following is the best-recognised indication for CT myelography rather than MRI?
options: First-line assessment of a young patient with acute sciatica
A patient with extensive lumbar spinal metalwork causing MRI artefact
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: A patient with extensive lumbar spinal metalwork causing MRI artefact
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: MRI is first-line for spinal soft-tissue and root pathology. CT myelography is reserved for patients who cannot have MRI (implants such as a pacemaker), severe claustrophobia, metal hardware causing MRI artefact, or where MRI is equivocal. Spinal metalwork blooms on MRI and obscures the canal, so CT myelography is a logical alternative.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: Before performing a myelogram via lumbar puncture, which precaution is most important to avoid catastrophic harm?
options: Exclude raised intracranial pressure / mass lesion (image the brain first) to avoid coning
Ensure the patient has fasted for 12 hours
Give prophylactic broad-spectrum IV antibiotics to all patients
Withhold the procedure unless the platelet count is above 400
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Exclude raised intracranial pressure / mass lesion (image the brain first) to avoid coning
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in raised intracranial pressure or a mass lesion because of the risk of cerebral herniation (coning); the brain should be imaged first. Other genuine risks include post-LP headache, infection (meningitis), bleeding, seizures (avoid drugs lowering the seizure threshold) and contrast reaction, but the coning risk is the immediately life-threatening one to exclude.

investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.question: An NG tube aspirate cannot be obtained. A CXR shows the tube passing down the left main bronchus into the lung. What is the correct action?
options: Feed cautiously at a low rate
Flush with water and use it
Remove the tube and re-site it — do not feed
Advance the tube 10 cm and feed
Confirm with a whoosh test then feed
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.answer: Remove the tube and re-site it — do not feed
investigations__PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY.explanation: The tube is in the lung. Feeding a misplaced NG tube is a Never Event. Remove and re-site, then re-confirm position (pH aspirate ≤5.5, or CXR showing the tube bisecting the carina with the tip below the left hemidiaphragm) before any feed.
